subsubtopic: SCRUTINY OF REGULATIONS-THIRD REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to table the third report of the Standing Committee on the Scrutiny of Regulations.
It is my duty to inform the House that this report contains a resolution pursuant to Standing Order 123 for the disallowance of sections 8, 13, 14 and 15 of the Indian health regulations, chapter 955 of the 1978 Consolidated Regulations of Canada. The text of the section subject to disallowance is included in Appendix A to this report.
Pursuant to Standing Order 35(1), I would like to give a succinct explanation of the procedure here. In the view of the committee the Indian health regulations contain provisions not authorized by the legislation passed by Parliament, as well as provisions that derogate from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the Canadian Bill of Rights.
Furthermore, the joint committee believes these same provisions contravene its scrutiny criterion No. 9 as they trespass unduly on the rights and liberties and its scrutiny criterion No. 10 in that they make the rights and liberties of the person unduly dependent on administrative discretion and are not consistent with the rules of natural justice.
These provisions would authorize government officials to order the arrest, detention and forcible medical treatment of Canadian citizens without judicial authorization.
Other provisions provide officials with an unfettered right of entry into private residences and with the
authority to order the destruction of premises without prior notice.
Faced with the reluctance of responsible departments to revoke these regulations, the committee which I have the privilege to chair with Senator Norman Grimard and my colleague, the hon. member for Red Deer, has no choice but to resolve that these regulations be revoked.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to send a powerful message of deterrence to anyone thinking of taking a gun along to commit a crime.
This bill would toughen section 85 of the Criminal Code, the section which makes it an offence to use a firearm while committing a crime. The minimum mandatory sentence would be increased from one to five years for a first offence and raised from three to eight years for any subsequent offences.

November 19, 1991
Routine Proceedings
Under this bill there would be no eligibility for parole. The bill also specifically prevents a mandatory sentence from having any impact on the sentence imposed for the other offence. The bill specifically requires the consent of the provincial Attorney General before any section 85 charge could be withdrawn or plea bargained away.
This idea is not new. It was proposed by former Prime Minister of Canada John Diefenbaker. I have talked to many police chiefs across Canada who are enthusiastic about this bill and wish it well.

Mr. Speaker, I have three petitions to present today.
The first is on behalf of a number of residents of the city of Kamloops, British Columbia. They urge the government to consider maintaining proper financial support for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to enable the RCMP to fulfil its mandate and role as the only visible police force for communities across British Columbia and of course remain as a viable symbol of Canadian unity at this critical time in our history.

Mr. Speaker, I have another petition to present.
The petitioners are from a number of western Canadian communities but primarily from British Columbia. They point out a number of concerns regarding the bid by Unitel to compete with Canada's telephone companies in long distance services.
They are concerned about the possibility of increased local costs and ask that the Minister of Communications hold information hearings in our communities before deciding the fate of Canada's telecommunications system. They acknowledge of course that cabinet would have the final decision if there is an appeal.

Mr. Speaker, I have a third petition to present on another topic. It is from residents of Kamloops, Vernon, Kelowna and other communities throughout the Okanagan Valley.
They point out their concern regarding a proposal to dam the North Thompson River at Valemount. That is a tributary of the Fraser River. The proponent wants to divert part of the river into the United States and eventually into the San Diego, California area.
They are simply calling upon the Government of Canada to state that it will not permit this project to proceed.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present to you and the House of Commons today a petition on education.

I have several petitioners here who point out that the government speaks about learning culture and about competitiveness, but what does it do? There have been cuts of almost half a billion dollars this year. This is quite apart from the impact of the goods and services tax on a number of services and products that the students need, as well as the 3 per cent administrative fee.
They deplore the government's actions and would like to see the government take a pro-active stance and give some leadership.

I support this petition and I promise to try to do what I can to help bring it about.

Mr. Speaker, I have a petition signed by over 200 Canadians from Saskatchewan communities such as Gainsborough, Oxbow, Domremy, Shaunavon, Weyburn, Moose Jaw, and Nova Scotia communities such as Wolfville and Falmouth and Westfield, New Brunswick.
November 19, 1991

These people are saying enough is enough when it comes to the erosion of the rural way of life, particularly the closure of rural post offices.
They are calling on Parliament to support Canada's rural way of life, to support the maintenance of rural post offices and postal services, and to reject the Conservative government's agenda of cutbacks and closures.

The House resumed from Monday, November 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bouchard (Roberval) that Bill C-39, an act to amend the Canada Pension Plan, the Family Allowances Act and the Old Age Security Act, be read the second time and referred to Legislative Committee B.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Ottawa South has the floor for 14 minutes.

Mr. Speaker, as I was about to complete my remarks last night, I was explaining that many people of my generation are afraid that this pension system will not continue until our old age. In fact, I support this bill because it is very important for us to have confidence that when we reach that age.
Government Orders
we will be entitled to receive benefits from the pension program.

I think it is essential to the maintenance of the Canadian system of social benefits, the entire network, that all Canadians believe they have a stake in the functioning and the long-term health of each of these programs, be it the Canada Pension Plan, medicare, old age security benefits and so on. The confidence must exist that no matter who you are, where you live in Canada or what your current economic condition is, you can contribute to these plans confident that they will benefit you in the long term as well.
That is the essence of the social contract which historically we as Canadians have been capable of building. I think it is crucial to the ongoing existence of our social programs as part of our framework.
I do want to use this occasion to make some comments, however, about my concerns about the increased reliance at all levels of government on payroll taxes and on other taxes that are not related to profitability as they apply to businesses in Canada.
The Canada Pension Plan of course was established at a time when payroll taxes were very much the exception rather than the rule. We understand that this system of employer-employee contributions to a funded pay as you go plan that is actuarially sound is essentially part of our system. However in the meantime since the 1960s the increased importance of payroll taxes, particularly in Canada compared to the United States, is becoming a problem especially for small and medium sized firms.
A study of taxation for small firms prepared by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business about this time last year entitled Taxing Ourselves to Death highlighted this concern. Let me quote from that report, which says that total payroll and local taxes which are not proportional to profitability account for about 30 per cent of the total tax burden for large firms in most jurisdictions, compared to more than 60 per cent for small businesses. Taxation studies in Ontario and five states were part of this study and put small businesses at a serious disadvantage in this respect, especially at times like the present when profits are low.

November 19, 1991
Government Orders
There are two points here. When you look at the burden of payroll taxes on small firms you have to include, of course, the Canada Pension Plan employer contributions we are discussing in this legislation.
Small firms are also confronted with payroll taxes based on the number of employees and the payrolls they provide with respect to unemployment insurance contributions. We have an indication in this House that the employer contributions are about to be increased significantly as well.
In the provinces there is the imposition of workmen's compensation premiums on firms, again based not on profitability, but on the payroll that is supported by the firm. In several provinces, particularly in Ontario, the cost of the health program is funded by employers through an employer tax. The employer health tax in Ontario is a payroll tax.
Therefore, the combination of all of these taxes, plus municipal tax rates which again are not related to a firm's profitability, impose an onerous burden, especially on small and medium-sized business.
Setting aside municipal taxes for a moment, when you impose heavier payroll taxes what you are essentially doing is encouraging firms to limit the number of people that they employ. In many cases, depending on what an employee's wage level is, it is better for a firm to encourage its existing staff to work overtime, to work longer hours, than to hire a new employee. The moment you bring the new employee through the door, you have an increased tax and paper burden that you have to bear.
Canada at the present time is struggling with unemployment rates well over 10 per cent. We have almost 1.5 million Canadians unemployed. Concerned as I am about the actuarial soundness of the Canada Pension Plan, it seems to me that it would be wise for this or any other government at the provincial level to look for ways to mitigate the burden of payroll taxes at a time when unemployment is such an acute problem.
Second, as the quotation from the Canadian Federation of Independent Business points out, this burden is disproportionately heavy on small and medium-sized firms. For example, if we look at the Ontario Premiers Council study done a couple of years ago at Canada in the world and the need for Canadian firms to compete internationally, the conclusion we have to come to is that
we are constantly struggling with the question of how we take our small firms and grow them into medium-sized firms, how we take our medium-sized firms and grow them into large international trading concerns. That should be our objective. The government wants consultation on prosperity. It seems to me that these studies have already been done and that is what they tell us.
If that is what we want to do and if that is what we need to accomplish in order to ensure the continuing prosperity of the people of our country, why would we simultaneously be devising tax systems that negatively affect just the kind of firms we are trying to make grow. We are shooting ourselves in the foot with our continued reliance on payroll taxes as a method of paying our costs as we go along. I wanted to express that concern.
Another concern that I have about the Canada Pension Plan is the use that the fund itself has historically been put to and continues to be put to in Canada. Unlike the province of Quebec that established its own pension fund as part of the Quebec Pension Plan, now operated by the Caisse de Depot in Quebec, the Canada Pension Plan has used its resources, not to grow them as well as possible, but essentially to lend money at preferred rates to the provinces of Canada. That may have made sense at the time, but when you contrast the effect that the Caisse de Depot has had in Quebec with what has occurred as a result of the investments made by the Canada Pension Plan, frankly the federal plan comes up short. I think that Quebec has demonstrated to us what a mixed economy can really accomplish.
If you take a government plan, and use it as an engine of growth in the economy, some amazing things can be achieved. The existence and the subsequent growth of many well-established Quebec firms as international competitors is in no small part due to the role that has been played over the last decades by the Caisse de Depot.
In Canada we have taken the contributions of employers and employees to the Canada Pension Plan, put them aside in a fund and generally loaned the money to provincial governments at slightly less than market rates.
It has been fine for the provincial governments and I suppose the theory is that since the loans are made available in proportion to the contributions made to the plan that really the contributors are benefiting through somewhat lower provincial tax rates at the time the loans are being made.

Since we are here today to discuss the soundness of this plan, you have to wonder whether the kind of mixed policy objective that gives a bit of saving today very indirectly through perhaps a mitigation of provincial taxes is really worth while in the long run when what we should really be doing is saying: "Let's set this fund aside. Let's ensure that it does as well as possibly can be for the benefit of the contributors and the right to entitlement in the future". That seems to me a better approach.
I would urge the government to take it upon itself to look again at some of the basic principles that have been applied in the development of the CPP and its operation over the last two and a half decades and ask some fundamental questions.
Perhaps now is the time to begin moving away from that investment approach and to look to establishing at least a hybrid system in which part of the fund is invested in growth investments to the benefit not only of the contributors and future beneficiaries of the fund but also to the Canadian economy in which investment of this sort could well be used.
We have in Canada a tendency to suffer from a lack of research and development. We have difficulty raising investment capital particularly for Canadian firms that will do a great deal of research and development. Our performance of R and D has lagged behind our major competitors internationally, partly because our economy has been so heavily based upon resources and second, on branch plants, generally branches of U.S. firms which do their research close to head office.
What an opportunity we have with the vast resource that is flowing into the Canada Pension Plan to provide capital for the performance of future looking research and development for the benefit of Canada and also I believe for the benefit ultimately of the contributors and the beneficiaries of the Canada Pension Plan. Why are we not looking at some of these ideas?
My time is completed but I think it is not enough just to pass this legislation and pat ourselves on the back and say: "Fine, we're making the CPP sound for the baby boom generation. They're going to collect it after all".
Government Orders
Now is the opportunity to look closely at how we are doing things in this country and question all of the assumptions of the past and look now for ways to do things better and differently.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a comment and direct a question to my hon. friend from Ottawa South.
First I want to congratulate him for his spirited defence of the RRSP regime last evening and I certainly want to associate myself fully with his remarks in that regard.
I feel there is perhaps an omission within Bill C-39. It relates to the plight of disabled Canadians who have contributed, through their earnings, to the Canada Pension Plan fund and who are obliged to leave their employment as a result of the disability but who are unaware of the possibility of receiving a disability pension, Believe it or not, there are still some Canadians in that position. They are unaware of the possibility of securing the benefit themselves and have not heard about it from medical people or from nurses or from friends or from family. By the time they do learn of the opportunity their entitlement is dissolved or has expired as a result of the application of the test of recency rules which I think require that a person contribute two of the last three years, five of the last ten. If the disabled person has not applied for CPP in that timeframe they simply are out of the picture.
Bill C-39 goes part way. It gives an opportunity to those people who could not apply as a direct result of their incapacity to have an application made for them. Then in the discretion of the minister the application can, in essence, be backdated to the time of the disability. However, that is only for people who are under an incapacity.
I have a concern about those other Canadians who are genuinely disabled but who simply did not know about the availability of the disability pension. I wonder if my hon. friend would be supportive of an amendment to try to open up this provision of the act to enable those few Canadians who were unaware of their opportunity to have the right to have their application backdated.

Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, this is a matter that has arisen also in my experience of constituency work. There have been individuals who either were unaware, or for whatever reason, did not get their applications filed in a timely fashion. I have always thought that the CPP rules were strangely arbitrary when you compare them, for example, to the rules which apply to veterans benefits. The administration of veterans disability programs has been exceedingly generous in allowing veterans to come forward to make disability claims many years after war service, upon demonstration of medical evidence that the injuries suffered were as a result of war service.
Another incongruity, for example, is between the disability provisions of CPP and those of the government's own superannuation plans. I have encountered situations where people were approved for superannuation disability benefits but not for CPP benefits, although you would think the payer is essentially the same entity and the tests of eligibility should correspond.
It seems to me that an extension of a rigid time formula that restricts people from what they are entitled to receive is not a fair way to administer the plan. The only benefit of a time limit is the ability to evaluate the evidence and that can be overcome provided there are conditions imposed which ensure that when a person makes a claim, their claim relates to a disability that arose during the time of eligibility. It is simply a bridging mechanism to allow people to backdate their claims upon satisfactory evidence of when the disability arose. So I would support that notion entirely.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to spend the first part of my time in addressing the general aspects of Bill C-39 which I support. I would like to spend the latter part of my time in pointing out where I think some improvements might in fact be made.
Bill C-39 proposes a number of changes to the Canada Pension Plan. I think the most significant of them is the one to ensure the long-term stability of the plan and to increase the amount of the children's benefits. The opportunity to discuss the social safety net and the position of the Canada Pension Plan in that net is always welcomed.
The Canada Pension Plan is a program which has in the past served Canadians very well. I believe it will continue to do so in the future. It is a key component of
the retirement income system in the country. Along with other elements of the pension benefits system, it has been a part of pension reform in recent years.
The first tier or level of the retirement income system in Canada is the Old Age Security Program, which provides the basic old age pension to seniors. It also includes the income tested guaranteed income supplement for low income pensioners, the income tested spousal allowance for 60 to 64 year old spouses of pensioners, and the allowance for widowed spouses for all low income widowed persons in this near elderly group.
In short, the OAS program provides a minimum income guarantee to more than 3.1 million senior citizens in this country. Of these, 1.4 million are also receiving the GIS low income supplement.
The second tier of the retirement system in this country is the Canada Pension Plan. This not only provides retirement income but also includes income protection for plan members and their dependent families in the event of disability and/or death.
The Canada Pension Plan plays a key role in providing a limited replacement of earnings for employed and self-employed earners up to a ceiling related to the average wage. In 1991 almost 1.9 million Canadians are receiving retirement pensions under the CPP. Another
600,000	are receiving similar benefits under the companion Quebec Pension Plan.
The third tier of Canada's retirement income system is composed of private sector arrangements which include employer sponsored pension and insurance plans, RRSPs and other private savings and investments.
One of the thrusts of this government has been to try to encourage greater self-reliance among all Canadians. It is for that reason the government has encouraged the use of private investment vehicles and particularly registered retirement savings plans. RRSPs have been available for a number of years and the proportion of Canadian workers contributing to them has increased significantly in recent years.
To support the personal retirement income objectives of Canadians further the government has made changes to the Income Tax Act effective with the 1991 taxation year. This allows for increases in the cash limits for tax deductible RRSP contributions. For example, in 1991 the RRSP limit is $11,500 or 18 per cent of eligible earnings, whichever is the lesser.
November 19, 1991

With respect to the Old Age Security Program I think it is commendable that despite the difficult financial circumstances and the requirement to pay so much in the way of service charges on the accumulated national debt the benefit payments under this program including the GIS and the spousal and widowed person's allowances have remained fully indexed.
In 1989 the government did introduce the tax back of Old Age Security benefits as part of its deficit reduction strategy, but this taxing back applies only to those Canadians with taxable income in excess of $50,000. The phase-out takes place in those income levels between $50,000 and $75,000 of taxable income.
In 1984 the maximum GIS rate for single pensioners was increased by $50 a month. Another major policy initiative under the OAS program was the introduction of the allowance for widowed spouses in 1985.
It is also important to point out that the low income elderly were protected from any adverse impact of the goods and services tax introduced this year. Not only were the monthly GIS payments to these pensioners fully indexed, but GIS recipients also received the quarterly GST credit.
The Canada Pension Plan back in 1987 was the subject of a number of major amendments. It included a provision for flexible retirement which allowed CPP members to take actuarially adjusted retirement pensions at any time from ages 60 to 70. There was also the introduction of the pension sharing provision between spouses which allowed for the sharing of retirement pensions earned by each spouse during the marriage.
There was also the introduction of the comprehensive financing agenda which will ensure the plan's long-term solvency. Today we are seeing the effective application of this provision in the financing amendments which are at the heart of this bill.
Other improvements at the time included expansion of the credit splitting provisions of the plan and a substantial increase in disability benefits.
What is referred to by the minister as a minor amendment is an important one. What it would do is
Government Orders
protect the rights of those incapacitated contributors who cannot act on their own behalf and thus may not have applied in time for any Canada Pension Plan benefit. The indication is that this class of amendment has a minimal effect on cost but would clarify legislation, simplify its application and allow payment of benefits where eligibility is not currently possible.
It is in this area that I believe strongly that some improvements could be made to the bill. In this country there are several hundred and perhaps several thousand Canadians who contributed during the course of their employment to the Canada Pension Plan and had to leave their employment as a result of physical or mental disability.
Despite all of the elaborate devices for notification and despite the fact that most of us would view that eligibility as common knowledge, the fact nevertheless remains that there are some Canadians who would qualify for the disability pension but simply did not apply in time. They have therefore been denied the opportunity to receive the kind of coverage which they deserve, to which they are entitled and for which they paid through their contributions.
I am going to take the liberty of referring once again in this House to a particular constituent of mine who has kindly authorized me to use her name. She is Mrs. Donna Sinclair of Swift Current, Saskatchewan. I suspect the situation of Mrs. Sinclair is similar to that of a number of other Canadians who should be able to participate and who should be able to receive a disability pension.
Mrs. Sinclair paid into the Canada Pension Plan from its inception back in 1966. She paid in for 11 of the 13 years between 1966 and 1978. She became disabled through diabetes. It is pretty clear that it was a disability. Unfortunately one of her legs was amputated in 1978. This precluded her further ability to work. Somehow it was not until 1987 some eight or nine years later that she became aware of the fact that she may well have been entitled to a disability pension. At that time she applied and she was barred by the test of recency rules which were alluded to previously.

November 19, 1991
Government Orders
Despite the fact that during her working time she had contributed 11 out of 13 years and had worked pretty well continuously, she became eligible because of the passage of time and because she did not know that she became eligible. No one had brought it to her attention. I think members on all sides have a handful of these situations. I believe it is a situation that cries out for redress.
It is not that it has not been mentioned before. I believe it has been raised in this House on a number of occasions. I know that it was raised during the adjournment debate in October 1989 when I referred specifically to Mrs. Sinclair's case. At that time the response of the parliamentary secretary to the minister was that the hon. member knew that his request to open the act to make amendments involved a process which was complex and required considerable time. Major changes to the CPP require the approval of two-thirds of the provinces having two-thirds of the Canadian population as well as the approval of Parliament. However he says: "I assure the hon. member that should the act be reopened his recommendations will be taken into consideration". That was in October 1989.
In June 1989 a question was put to the then Minister of National Health and Welfare. He indicated among other things that the government had no current intention of reopening the Canada Pension Plan Act but that should that arise they would certainly take into consideration the recommendations of the hon. gentleman.
In the meantime it is obvious that the act has been reopened. Presumably there have been discussions with the provinces. I am not sure what has happened to the plight of these people. I do not think there are a great many of them but I believe their situation cries out for redress.
There was a report made to the Minister of National Health and Welfare by the Canada Pension Plan Advisory Board in May 1990. That advisory body did make a statement in its wisdom. It is not a lengthy report. It is just six pages in length. The matter of the late applications was dealt with very briefly. I quote from page 4:
Given that the disability benefit is intended to replace lost earnings, that the recency retroactivity provisions are generous and that most individuals apply within the time allowed, the committee did not see that there was any need to liberalize the provisions.
With the greatest respect I find myself in disagreement with this conclusion. The fact that most individuals apply within the time allowed certainly does not solve the problem for those who through no fault of their own simply did not know about the opportunity and did not apply. It seems to me that the whole thrust of our social safety net is to ensure a certain level of income for people who have contributed. This woman and many others in her position have contributed to the system, and I think are deserving of receiving benefits from it.
I want to congratulate the government for acting on one of the recommendations, that the act be amended to grant late applicants the right to appeal on the basis they were incapable of applying for the disability benefit within the normal time limit. That is certainly beyond question. The person may have been unable to apply because of a mental incapacity. Perhaps they were in a coma or whatever. Clearly someone ought to be able to apply on their behalf. I think that Canadians would find that fair and reasonable.
I suggest that the same consideration should be granted to all of those disabled Canadians who were disabled at the time of leaving their employment. In fact they left their employment as a result of the disability and simply did not know about the opportunity. Through the passage of time and the application of these test of recency rules they became ineligible. I think the situation cries out for attention and I see no better time than the present. What I want to do is urge the government to consider an amendment. Failing that I want to encourage the committee to entertain an amendment to widen this provision to allow for retroactivity in terms of application.
I do not believe for a moment that the number of Canadians involved are large but I think that the need of those particular people certainly is great. They have paid into the plan and there is absolutely no reason why they should not be entitled to be able to qualify upon the appropriate proof.
To return again to the Sinclair case, I might add that I believe this government did make a procedural change in 1985 which resulted in notice going out to potential Canada Pension Plan applicants advising them of their rights and advising them of the opportunity. Unfortunately, this was not in existence prior to 1985. So there was no way that these people would know other than I
November 19, 1991

guess through the work place, through advice from neighbours, friends, medical people and so on. In spite of a fairly elaborate system of notice, it is clear that there are still people who fall through the cracks, if you like, people who would otherwise qualify but for the passage of time. I would again like to strongly urge the consideration of this House on an amendment in that regard.
I should point out that the suggestion has been made that that the matter could be dealt with through Private Members' Business, but with all due respect, I think not. Several members have had bills and motions in the hopper, but as you know, Mr. Speaker, it is a bit of a game of chance. They may or may not be drawn for debate. They may or may not receive five hours of attention. They may or may not come to a vote.
I commend the hon. member for Don Valley East who has Bill C-280 on the table at the present time which would at least widen the opportunity for disabled people to apply. It would I believe lengthen the time and change the test of recency rules. The likelihood of that coming forward into a votable position is slim.
I think the time to deal with this matter is now. It is in front of the House and I detect sympathy on all sides for the position. It is not a big ticket item in terms of finances and I believe it calls for attention.
I would just like to conclude my remarks by saying that on balance, certainly I find the bill to be commendable and supportable. The increase in the child benefits is I think laudable. Making the Canada Pension Plan fiscally sound in future years I think is an absolute necessity.
All in all, I commend the minister for bringing forward these amendments but with the addendum that I think the matter of disabled Canadians does need attention. I do not think it is enough just to say that those who are incapacitated and incapable of making an application should be considered. I think all of those Canadians who were disabled, left their work as a result of disability, paid into the system, should have the opportunity to benefit by it.
Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his kind comments about my Private Member's Bill C-280, and also to thank him very much for his remarks indicating that he feels this particular bill, C-39, should be amended to include those provisions relating to the limitation period on disability pensions under the Canada Pension Plan. He and I have had a great many difficulties raised with us by constituents and I know all members of the House have as well.
I was interested particularly in his remarks that he had been told that when the bill was reopened this provision would be dealt with, the limitation period on disability pensions. I was told that same thing back in 1985. The hon. member was told in 1989. Just recently I was told again that the next time there was another round of Canada Pension Plan amendments, the government would be pleased to put this forward and this time finally deal with it.
I understand that my office was contacted just this morning and the staff of the minister is going to be meeting with me tomorrow. I am sure they will be urging me again to wait for the next round. I do not think that is good enough, especially after seven or eight years of waiting now.
I want to ask the hon. member if he believes that one of the reasons that Canadians have lost confidence in politicians, have lost confidence in members of Parliament and have lost confidence in government is because of situations like this where all of us are inclined to listen to departmental staff, listen to ministers' staffs, wait, wait, wait for things that never come about, things which then the staff says were the fault of some other minister's staff and not their fault, just wait until the next time and things will be different. Does the hon. member agree with me that this is one of the Bbig reasons why Canadians are losing confidence with the political process?

Mr. Speaker, it is hard to disagree with the position put by my colleague from Don Valley East.
I think part of the problem is that governments tend to do the big ticket items quite well, but there are a number of the little things that perhaps are left aside or are not considered important enough or perhaps fall in the cracks.

November 19, 1991
Government Orders
The number of people who would be affected by this minor amendment to the Canada Pension Plan legislation is probably in the hundreds or perhaps a few thousand. It is not a big ticket item at all. I think all that is required is the will to bring it forward for discussion.
It may well be that in a succession of ministers, that Mr. Epp, Mr. Beatty and, of course, our present minister, and I do not particularly fault them, but ministers come and go, members of Parliament come and go, but I think that bureaucracy tends to stay. They are the people who wrote the speeches and wrote the responses for the parliamentary secretary and said: "Yes, it will be dealt with". They are the ones who are here on an ongoing basis. But the fact is that when it comes time they, for whatever reasons, apparently choose not to deal with it.
I agree with the hon. member that putting it off is not good enough. I strongly urge members on all sides to seize this opportunity now in order to redress this problem. If it is not done now, it is quite clear that it will be put off again and again and again. The bureaucracy may view it as something small and it does not matter, there are only a few hundred people and it is not that important, but for those few hundred people it is awfully important. I think for Canadians generally it is important that the principles and the integrity of our social safety net be insured and that those benefits be available for all. It is not good enough for the bureaucrats and for the departmental people to hide out behind the regulations.
Just with reference to Mrs. Sinclair and her case that I mentioned earlier in my remarks, the fact is that she did appeal the denial, as is her right, to a tribunal composed of three people, the government representative, her own representative and a chairperson. Indeed those three people earlier this year unanimously said: "Yes, of course this woman should qualify." They cited charter reasons and they cited simple justice, if you like. But, of course, the departmental people, the bureaucrats in their wisdom have seen fit to appeal this. It is not good enough that the lay board said that of course the woman should qualify. Our bureaucrats are out there saying: "Well here is the rule, the test of recency, and by gosh the fact that you paid in and the fact that you are disabled and the fact that you need this means not a damn thing".
It is pretty clear that the bureaucrats are going to say: "Well here is this Pension Plan Advisory Board report and there is this problem, budgetary problems and all the rest of it". They will find a million excuses, but the fact remains that there is a woman out there, I guess there are hundreds of Canadians out there who have paid in, are disabled, have a need, who are entitled and who should receive the benefits. The bureaucrats are not going to get those benefits to them. It is up to the elected representatives of the Canadian people in this place to ensure that it happens.

Mr. Speaker, speaking of rights, since those who have contributed have developed an inherent right to the plan, whether they are claiming disability benefits or the simple retirement pension plan benefits, would the member agree that as a matter of right, when a contributor has failed to file in time he should not be penalized. The automatic penalty is the interest on the benefits that the contributor has lost, but the inherent right to get those benefits must always be with the contributor and therefore the statutory limit as to the date of application perhaps is archaic and has to be abolished completely.

Mr. Speaker, I apologize. I didn't realize I was supposed to give the hon. member a chance to ask his question. Now I understand.
The first comment I want to make is that I am a little sensitive to the fact that it is easy for politicians to blame the civil service for lack of action. It is a very convenient scapegoat.
I have some sensitivity there. In fact, I have often said that it is unfortunate that we do not appreciate the quality of the civil servant. Perhaps we do not use them as well as we might in order to get the kinds of things that we want done.
Translation]


November 19, 1991

Very often, we fail to articulate what it is that we want done in terms that the civil service can in fact follow up on. I just wanted to make that point because I think that the civil service is too often maligned.
I am pleased to be able to stand in the House today to talk about an act to amend the Canada Pension Plan, the Family Allowances Act and the Old Age Security Act. What is in fact being done here? First of all, the major goal appears to be one where you want to ensure that there is solvency in this particular plan. I have no particular difficulties with that, but I want to probe it just a bit.
Second, there will be more benefits for children, and I am absolutely delighted. I think it is something that should have happened some time ago. Thank goodness it is about to happen.
There will be some additional provisions, and I applaud that as well, for incapacitated or disabled Canadians. I think there needs to be more work done in that area. At the very least, these Canadians-the others as well-need to know in very clear, simple language what it is that is available to them.
Those particular provisions are often extremely confusing. They are described in language that is not terribly clear. I am not suggesting that people are intentionally doing that. It is a reality and I hope we could come to grips with that.
The notion of credit splitting is something that is past due. I am pleased that this is in fact happening now. I think it is a positive measure. Of course, there is administrative streamlining.
While I see that as a potential benefit, I am always a little suspicious that when we administratively streamline something there may be some other motivation there, for example, to see whether or not we can move funds about from one program to another. If it is to save money but not at the expense of Canadians that need it, then I applaud it. If it has additional motivations, then I am not at all pleased.
Let me address the question of solvency because I think it is an extremely important one. In fact, it appears to be the major goal of the government with respect to this particular project. It is to ensure that this particular
Government Orders
plan will be self-sufficient, that there will not be any deficits and that it will be able to pay for itself.
When the government suggests that this needs to be done now, it gives three reasons. It is because, it says, of declining birth rates, diminishing worker productivity and early retirement. These are all realities, but at the same time it does not go any further and I am not surprised.
It has not talked about the unemployed people in Canada, the almost 1.5 million who are not in a position to be able to contribute to this fund. It has not talked about the difficulties in the economy which has not only created unemployed Canadians, but has also brought about a downsizing to the economy and has given many Canadians very little choice but to take early retirement.
Those are other reasons why this particular program finds itself short of funds. It has in fact been caused in part by the mismanagement of the national economy by the government. I do not say that unkindly. I think if one looks at the facts in a very rational kind of way, one will know that that is exactly true.
I want to review why the government is doing this. It is to ensure the continued good health of the Canada Pension Plan and for the provision of increased benefits for 170,000 children of deceased plan participants and benefits that will grow from $113 to $148 a month. I think that is very positive, and I applaud those measures.
I also want to point out, and I do not do so maliciously, that this is another tax. Whether you like it or not, you, I and many others will have to pay more. Therefore, it is another tax.
An interesting observation was made in February 1991 by Stewart MacLeod of the Thomson News Service. He pointed out that this kind of tax, this kind of user fee, was the third most important source of revenue for government today after income tax and sales tax. You can cloak it in all kinds of neat phrases and what have you, but it is still a tax and it should in fact be admitted that this is so. As I pointed out, it is the third most important source of revenue in Canada today.
The other observation I want make is as follows. [Translation]
We have no guarantees at all that this increase in contribution rates will be enough. No one can guarantee

November 19, 1991
Government Orders
that. In fact, we realize this increase may not be enough and that there may be further major problems with financing.
As you know, the provinces borrow money at a preferential rate, and they will continue to do so. If we consider the preferential rate enjoyed by the provinces, it is clear this also tends to reduce the amount of money available to the fund and in no way contributes to its stability.

I really feel very strongly that there needs to be an over-all review of this whole plan including this plan in terms of the other social programs available to Canadians. Of course the appropriate question would be why.
Let me quote from an article that I think makes the point most eloquently. It says, and I want to quote it directly: "We believe it is fundamentally wrong that a public pension program set up to cover the entire paid labour force is incapable of producing benefits large enough to keep most of its beneficiaries out of poverty". That is from the pension reform report of the National Council on Welfare of last February.
That is the major issue. This particular pension plan does not address a number of the actual issues that exist in Canada today. Let us talk briefly about that social scene.

Right here in Canada, about five million people live in poverty. Most of them are women, and one million are children. We know that today two million Canadians are on welfare, and that 1.8 million Canadians, including a high percentage of children will be fed by food banks. If I remember correctly, the proportion of children and young people is around 40 per cent.
At this very moment, nearly 1.5 million people are unemployed. How will these people be affected by these adjustments?

I think we have to realize that the assumptions have changed since this program was put afoot, since it was set up. Therefore we need to re-examine it right from the very beginning and some of the realities we have to deal with.
For example, there are more early retirements today. Perhaps it is as a result of a faltering economy or changing lifestyles and demographics or combinations thereof. There are fewer births than there were. Immigration patterns have changed. Work force patterns have changed.
Therefore I think it is absolutely essential to look at this particular program to see if it is as sound as it might be, not only from a financial perspective but in terms of responding to the needs of Canadians, and to see how it dovetails, how it fits with the other social programs in Canada so that we can have as effective a program as possible to respond to the real needs of Canadians.
Let me just make a few more points. I think all of us would admit-and I believe all members who have spoken today from all parties have indicated it-that these plans are still not doing a good enough job. They are in fact meeting a lot of needs of a lot of Canadians and that is very important. Surely our purpose in government is to continue to perfect those plans, to ensure that we have removed the glitches, to make them better than what they were and continue to improve upon them.
The question I would like to ask is: Where is the study that has examined all of the various situations which have been brought to the attention of the government and have been referred to in some of the addresses today. They identify some of the real difficulties that Canadians are having. Therefore, where is the response to this study?

Unfortunately, there is no such study, and the adjustments being made now, favourable though they may be, fail to focus on the real problems facing Canadians today.

I would have thought that one of the first things we would have done is ensure the solvency of this particular program, that we would have identified Canadians throughout the land who are experiencing difficulties, and that we would have brought about remedial procedures in order to correct those particular limitations. That is sadly lacking and it is really unfortunate. I would hope in the near future that something might be done.

What we really need in Canada is an examination of this plan. We need to examine its fundamental assumptions. We need to come to grips with new realities. We need to look at it in juxtaposition to other programs. We need to make, it seems to me, two commitments that are fundamental. The first commitment is that we want adequate protection for all Canadians who need this kind of assistance. I think all of us would say that. We need to debate openly the amount of protection and the kind of protection that Canadians should enjoy. Of course we need to make a commitment to have solvent plan.
Mr. Speaker, you and I both know that investments today will in fact make sure that happens in the future. However, I am really quite concerned about investments that perhaps do not address the realities of today or tomorrow.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps I may give a brief summary. First of all, I welcome certain changes, up to a point. I think financial stability is absolutely essential. I approve of certain administrative changes, but I want to make it quite clear that I hope the purpose of these changes is to simplify procedures, not to take advantage of people or situations.
There are other measures that are excellent, and I am very pleased about that. But I repeat, it is extremely important to take a close look at the real problems I just identified and ensure there is a plan that will deal with these problems. Otherwise we may go on like this for a couple of years, making adjustments here and there without really finding a solution to the real problems the program is expected to deal with.

I am pleased that I have had an opportunity to say a few words about these important changes. Once again I think it is important to re-examine it from the very basis to ensure that it does the job that it needs to do, to examine the assumptions, the new realities, and to come forward with a commitment, a commitment from all parliamentarians that we need to address the financial and real needs of Canadians. We need to do it in a
Government Orders
responsible financial kind of way, but that should not prevent us from going forward now.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate my colleague from St. Boniface for a well laid out presentation.
I would like to put on the record that I support the bill in principle first of all because it is attempting to ensure the good health of the Canada Pension Plan. It also has increased the benefits for children of deceased plan participants.
However I do have some concerns like my hon. colleague. I want to mention them and perhaps ask my colleague if he could comment on them. One of the areas of concern is that the citizens of Canada are fed up with paying more taxes. That goes for all classes of society. In this case when we look at increased premiums for the Canada Pension Plan, it is a form of another tax.
I would hope that the committee when it re-examines this bill will look at the impact of increased costs on modest and low income workers.
Another area we forget about quite often is the small business community, the small business sector across Canada that is feeling the pinch now and is faced with many expenses, especially in this time of recession. We see an increase in UIC premiums which again is another form of tax. Now we are talking about increases in Canada Pension Plan premiums. I believe we have to take that into account and make some recommendations to help these special sectors of our Canadian economy.
Another point I would like to make is perhaps one the hon. member did make. I would like him to reinforce it for us. It concerns the management of the fund. I think Canadians have to feel confident that the Canada Pension Plan is a well managed fund. I hope the hon. member would mention additional points on that issue.
I have a personal concern. Since becoming a member of Parliament I have been involved with a number of cases with respect to applications for disability pensions. I find that there seems to be a lack of compassion in the interpretation of the rules, a lack of flexibility, and a lack of definition with regard to the disability criteria clause dealing with prolonged and severe disability. I was

November 19, 1991
Government Orders
hoping that the government would address this issue in Bill C-39, but I guess it does not intend to do that.
I would also ask my hon. colleague to comment on whether he feels there should be no penalty for early retirement and that there should be no statutory limit on the date of application. I certainly feel very strongly with regard to those two items.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague has raised a number of questions, and I thank him for each and every one of them.
First of all, turning to the well managed plan, it is absolutely essential. Otherwise we would lose confidence. Of course a loss of confidence is what I think could probably undermine it quite apart from insolvency. We need to ensure that the people managing it are doing so with openness and that the sharing of information is a reality. We as Canadians must have confidence that when the time comes for us and others to retire the situation will be as we have been led to believe it will be. That is a very important point.
I appreciate as well the reference to low and modest income earners and small business people, because it will impact significantly upon them. There is no doubt about that. I think we have to be particularly sensitive to them as well as to the middle class which in a sense is the motor of an economy such as ours. However, it has been so crushed by tax after tax, well over 30 right now, that that motor is not running well. Of course therein lies some of our problems, our economic instability, our unemployment and other kinds of difficulties as well.
The point is well taken. This is another tax. As I mentioned before, this is the third most important source of revenue for governments today. In other words, it raises more money than a number of other sources, only surpassed by income and sales taxes. It is a tax. We can cloak it in whatever kind of language we want, put little ribbons on it or what have you, but it is a tax that will affect all Canadians. Because the tax impositions have been so significant and so numerous during the last few years definitely there is some real concern.
The lack of definitions is a particularly good point as well. The member is quite right. It has perhaps been my greatest challenge as a member of Parliament in terms of
cases that I handle. I think it is easy to blame the bureaucracy, but the politicians who are in power know that this is a problem. They should tell the bureaucrats to come up with definitions that they can examine as people who govern and then say whether it is right or wrong or whether they need some additional work done.
I am a little worried about the cop-out that is being exercised here. We know some of those problems. People on the government side know what some of those problems are. Therefore I think it is very important for them to get the people to define, identify the problems, bring forward solutions and then choose them.
I have two other very quick reactions. Turning to no penalty for early retirement, I think that is something we should look at for the entire Canadian population. It would require some additional investments on the part of the worker. I applaud that in a philosophical sense. I would have to look at it very carefully. Certainly I think it should be available for Canadians. I would obviously like to see it solved.
One final point I believe is the question of retroactive benefits. It is one of the problems we have today. I met an 81-year old gentleman who did not know he was entitled to a certain program, and he got retroactive benefits for three years. He could have received them for 15, 16 or more years. I met a war widow who found out that she was entitled to two particular financial programs. She got retroactive benefits for one year in one instance and I think for three years in the other. It does not matter. She had been without that kind of support for 20 years. She had lost her house, raised her children and had a whole lot of difficulties.
I do not think it is fair to say to Canadians who were not aware of this-because some of them are not in a good enough state of health to be aware-that they have to pay the penalty. I think they should be entitled to it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity today to take part in the debate on Bill C-39, an act to amend the Canada Pension Plan, the Family Allowances Act and the Old Age Security Act.
November 19, 1991

I would like to start by congratulating more specifically my colleague from Winnipeg North who led off the debate on this bill for the Liberals. He did an excellent job, as always, Mr. Speaker.
Bill C-39, introduced by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, is an ambitious and complex piece of legislation, as pointed out by the hon. member for Winnipeg North, who gave his analysis of the bill while explaining our party's position. Since my speaking time is limited, I would prefer to comment on some of the highlights of this bill.
The purpose of this bill is to make a number of changes in the Canada Pension Plan. The government tells us it has to raise contribution rates for employers and employees to ensure that the Canada Pension Plan fund is maintained at a satisfactory level. According to the government, these changes are intended to improve the financial position of the plan. At the present time, the contribution rate for employers and employees is 4.6 per cent. Under the proposed legislation, the government intends to double this contribution by the year 2011.
Mr. Speaker, you and I are both from the province of Quebec. I represent the riding of Saint-Leonard, and of course we have our own pension plan: the Quebec Pension Plan. However, the changes proposed in this bill will also oblige the Quebec government to raise the contribution rate in its own plan. In fact, I think it has already announced that it intends to do just that. As I was saying, even if we in Quebec do not have the Canada Pension Plan but our own Quebec Pension Plan, what we are doing here will be extremely important for Quebec.
The government is increasing the contribution rate for several reasons. Some of them I support. Of course, we have to ensure the Canada Pension Plan remains financially sound. But here again, and I repeat what I said yesterday in referring to unemployment insurance premiums, we have another tax increase. I agree, this is about the Canada Pension Plan, the Quebec Pension Plan and the Family Allowances Act, not unemployment insurance, but the problem is the same. Every time we raise the contribution rate for the Canada Pension Plan or the Quebec Pension Plan or unemployment insurance, we increase the tax burden on workers and
Government Orders
employers. Considering the current state of the economy, such increases are difficult to justify.
The government says that the unemployed do not receive benefits under the plan and are thus not affected by these increases. That is true. But we must not forget that at the same time, the unemployed do not contribute to the plan because the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan are based on wage earnings.
So those who do not work do not contribute to this program. The present economic situation has not helped the Canada Pension Plan. As the government admitted yesterday, the unemployment insurance fund is running a huge deficit because of the recession. More people are receiving unemployment insurance benefits, but fewer are contributing because the contribution system is based on work. People who do not work do not contribute to the plan and neither do employers so that automatically puts the plan in difficulty.
When the minister tells us that the economic situation is not to blame for higher rates, I do not quite agree with him, because the economic situation has a direct effect on the pension plan.
The Conservative government is responsible for the economic slump. I am not the only one saying that; Canadian leaders have also said so. It is because of the monetary policy, the GST, the free trade treaty with the United States. The government must shoulder its responsibilities. When things go well, the government takes every opportunity to rise in this House to say so. But today it must face up to its responsibilities. It is responsible for having to raise contributions to the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans. The government should have presented Canadians with economic policies to keep these pension funds and the whole economy alive, instead of having so many bankruptcies. The bankruptcy statistics show that it is completely out of control, that unemployment is rising and that we have a financial problem.
I have still not talked about where small and mediumsized businesses fit into this. Imagine what it will do to small and medium-sized businesses. An analysis of all sectors of the economy and of self-employed workers shows that 50 per cent of workers in Canada work in small and medium-sized businesses; 92.7 per cent of the businesses in Canada fit into that category, since they

November 19, 1991
Government Orders
have fewer than 50 employees; 97.2 of businesses have 100 employees or less.
So when you add the increase that the Minister of National Health and Welfare imposed on us to the 7.1 per cent increase that the Minister of Employment and Immigration announced yesterday for unemployment insurance premiums, you realize that it is a very heavy burden at a time when everyone-workers, employers, small business people-is trying to revive the economy. Everybody is doing all they can to keep at least the existing jobs and to create new ones. We know that small and medium-sized businesses create 80 per cent of the jobs.
Since yesterday the comments from all quarters, management or labour, tell us that this is not the right time-it is time to encourage people to create jobs. If we want to encourage job creation, knowing that small and medium-sized businesses create 80 per cent of our jobs, that is precisely the sector that cannot pay such increases, that cannot afford them. That is why I say the timing is wrong. It is not the right time for an increase.
Of course I must admit that I agree with some things in the bill. For example, Bill C-39 proposes a $35 increase in benefits for dependent children of deceased or disabled contributors. There are some 170,000 children of deceased or disabled contributors in the country and no one can criticize an effort to help them in these difficult times.
Therefore, I do not want to give the impression that I am only criticizing. When the government does good things, I say so and I congratulate them. I also believe, and my colleague from Winnipeg North has said the same thing, as well as all my other colleagues who participated in this debate, that it is not true that the opposition only criticizes the government, because we also point out the good things it does. Unfortunately, the government does not do enough good things.
We are now trying to get out of a recession and it is not by imposing new taxes or by increasing existing ones that we will do that.
As I was saying, this bill has some good points but it is yet another tax at a bad time. The employers and workers of the country are the driving force of our
economy, but their purchasing power is continually being eroded, thus keeping our economy in a recession. In 1991 alone, there has been the GST, a 24 per cent increase in unemployment insurance premiums, and many other taxes, duties and fees. There are many hidden taxes. If one wants to apply to the immigration office for a relative to come to Canada, it costs $250 just to open the file. That is another tax.
It all adds up to quite a lot. I for one seriously wonder if the government's advisers really think about it, because the whole monetary policy of the government is aimed at reducing inflation. If we look at what causes inflation and eliminate everything produced, everything necessary, we realize that our inflation is caused by taxes. So on the one hand, the government keeps the dollar and interest rates high-of course now they are coming down, and I agree, but before going down, they went up and we must not forget that. The government brought the dollar and interest rates up and now it is bringing them down. After putting us in an untenable economic situation, it has now started to lower interest rates, yet we have said for a long time that these rates must come down.
Monetary policy was used to bring down inflation, but you cannot do that by penalizing businesses and consumers with taxes, because these taxes only serve to bring the inflation rate up. Therefore, there is a contradiction in the government's economic policies and I hope that advisers and the government itself will look at this situation, will stop taxing Canadians and instead try to help them out of this economic slump. Then we will be able to look at all our social programs to keep them sound, because nobody is opposed to keeping this pension plan healthy.
We of course support this bill in principle, as I said, but we nevertheless want to review it thoroughly in committee in order to find solutions and propose amendments. I also submit to my colleague from Winnipeg North that perhaps we could look at the issue of disability pensions in Canada. I represent the riding of Saint-Leonard and I imagine, Mr. Speaker, that your riding like mine and the ridings of other hon. members across the country have to deal with disability cases. Under our system you must literally be at death's door to be eligible for a disability pension in Canada.
[DOT]'.ftA'
November 19, 1991

If a young person has a medical problem that keeps him from working, he has a lot of time ahead of him, but if sick or disabled person has reached a certain age there are problems. I remember the case of a 55-year-old man in my riding-at 60 you are eligible for pension plan benefits, even though the amount is reduced-who underwent a major operation and the doctor told him, he was a construction worker: "You will no longer be able to work in construction. You must find lighter work." Less strenuous, Mr. Speaker? How is someone who worked all his life in the construction industry going to find a less strenuous job?
The doctor says in his report that this person is ill and cannot work in the construction industry, but he doesn't say he is unfit to work. Automatically this means he does not qualify for and does not get his disability pension, which creates a very real financial problem for the family. It means he won't be able to keep his children in college or university.
I think we should take this opportunity to consider how we could improve the whole issue of disability and the CPP, because this is very important. I would say that 25 per cent of the cases I have in my riding concern disability pensions. Of course, there are a number of cases of work-related accidents which come under provincial jurisdiction. As I said earlier, in Quebec we have our own Quebec Pension Plan, but if certain changes are made in the federal plan, Quebec's provincial plan will certainly follow suit. In fact, when Quebec made pensions available starting at the age of 60, the federal government had not yet done so but subsequently took Quebec's lead.
As far as we are concerned, at the federal level, we should take a look at the whole issue of disability. This is very important in the kind of society we have today, because when we get a little older, we are told: You can't do your job any more because of an accident or because of illness, but you could work at another job. When you consider how competitive the labour market is today, once you get to be a certain age it is a lot harder. So we should let these people have a disability pension. Some people may be able to do less strenuous work, part time, to help the family budget and keep their children in university or college, since our young people need a good education.
There is a whole series of social programs we have to review and we must do so as soon as possible.

I do not know how much time I have left. I probably
Government Orders
have three minutes. I will try to summarize for my English speaking electors and constituents in my riding of St. Leonard even though in Quebec we have our own Quebec Pension Plan.
We are talking here about the Canada Pension Plan and increasing the premiums that employees and employers have to pay. We want to ensure that the Canada Pension Plan or the Quebec plan stays alive for a long time so that when the time comes we can all get our pensions. It is important and I agree that we should make sure that the program is alive and well financed.
Because of the economic situation that we are in I believe that the government should freeze premiums until we are in a better economic situation. The Quebec government has already indicated it will follow and freeze its premiums as well.
Yesterday's announcement of a 7.1 per cent increase in UI premiums will affect small businesses. Ninety per cent of businesses in Canada are small businesses. They will be affected very much. This will definitely not help them get out of the recession and create the jobs that we need so badly to get all the country out of the recession.
I would also like to talk about the disability part of the plan. There are a lot of people who through accident or sickness at age 50 or 55 hear the doctor say: "You cannot do the same work any more. Maybe you can do a light job". Taking into consideration the job market situation, it is very hard for a person of 50 or 55 years to adjust to a change of job when he has a physical disability.
In those cases we should look at the possibilities of allowing those people who are in need and suffering to get a disability pension before the age of 60. Then they can continue to look after their families and children who might be in college or university.
Thank you for your patience, Mr. Speaker. I realize my time has expired.
