speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)) moved
subtopic: TELESAT CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-38, an act to provide for the continuance of Telesat Canada under the Canada Business Corporations Act and for the disposal of the shares therein of Her Majesty in right of Canada, be read a second time and referred to Legislative Committee E.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to start debate on Bill C-38, an act that will enable the government to sell its shares in Telesat Canada.
Before speaking on the specifics of the legislation I would like to take a few minutes to discuss the government's privatization program and, within that context, the reason for our decision to sell the government's Telesat shares.
At the outset I think it is important to point out that Telesat Canada is not a Crown corporation. It is a mixed enterprise with public and private ownership. Therefore the sale of the government shares in the company is not technically a privatization of a Crown owned enterprise. However the principles of the privatization program do indeed apply to the proposed divestiture of the government's interests in Telesat.
When this government came to office in 1984 we inherited a fiscal situation that was described as being totally out of control. The deficit in 1984-85 was $38.5 billion. This consisted of $22.4 billion in interest on the accumulated debt to that date and $16.1 billion in operating deficits. In other words the government was spending $16 billion more on programs than it was receiving in revenues.
In contrast to the overspending of previous governments, this government stands for expenditure control and effective money management. Like any household, we realize that if your spending continues to sharply exceed your income, the bills keep piling up. That of course leads to serious financial difficulties.
The citizens of Canada have always known where this government stands on the fundamental issues. That is why they overwhelmingly elected us in 1984 and again in 1988. During this time we have achieved real fiscal progress.
As the February 1991 budget indicated, the deficit this year will be held despite the recession at $30.5 billion. The deficit would be substantially higher had we not through expenditure control turned the $16.1 billion operating deficit which we found in 1984 into a $12.5 billion surplus by fiscal year 1990-91. In other words we collected $12.5 billion more than we spent on programs.
November 19, 1991

In the next fiscal year, 1992-93, the deficit will fall below $25 billion and that is for the first time in a decade. By 1995-96 the deficit is forecast to decline to the $6 billion level or seven-tenths of one per cent of the Gross Domestic Product. By then the government will no longer be borrowing additional net funds in the financial markets. For the first time in a quarter of a century I might point out it will begin to buy back its bonds and the treasury bills known as that huge accumulated debt.
In pursuing our expenditure control program we have closely examined Crown corporations and other Crown investments. As members will recall the broad parameters of Canada's privatization program were first set out in the 1985 budget. At that time the then Minister of Finance announced our intention to review our inventory of Crown holdings with an eye to privatizing those commercially viable Canadian companies that no longer served a public policy purpose.

The time had come for the government to take steps reflecting the changes that had taken place during the past 30 or 40 years in Canada's economic and social infrastructure. As so often happens, the problems and priorities of the past had been dealt with, but new problems had arisen demanding new solutions.

In the past government ownership was a viable way of filling a private sector void protecting technology or contributing to nation building. By 1985 that was no longer the situation in many instances. Canada's economic and social infrastructures were relatively mature. The private sector was in a position to provide services once effectively delivered by the government. Moreover, in many cases the economy had the ability to grow and prosper without intrusive policies such as direct government participation in the economy.
Let me reiterate that the reduced need for Crown corporations to meet public policy goals can lead to a reduced drain on the federal Treasury. Given the fiscal quagmire that we inherited in 1984 and Canadians intense desire for more efficient management of public resources, the fiscal importance of the government's privatization program cannot be overstated.
Furthermore, privatizations will help reduce Canada's financial burden because all net proceeds from the sale of Crown corporations-and I want to make this veiy
Government Orders
clear-all net proceeds from the sale of Crown corporations will go into the debt servicing and reduction account, announced in the February budget and presently enshrined in legislation which is being debated at committee stage.
Although Telesat is not a Crown corporation, it is a company in which the government owns a controlling interest. Now I sit here and I watch the NDP sitting over there shaking their heads. I note that Bob Rae just privatized the Dome the other day. I see even the NDP is privatizing. The members sit over there and shake their heads, yet their brothers in the province are doing just that because they know it is the right thing to do.
Just to educate my hon. friend because obviously he does not know about Telesat, Telesat was set up in 1969 with three classes of shareholders; the government, telecommunications carriers and the public at large. It was not a Crown corporation, it was a mixed enterprise system. However, shares were never sold to the public but it was set up to do that. With the passage of Bill C-38 the government will be in position to sell 53 per cent of Telesat shares. It now owns 49.3 per cent of Telesat shares and 3.7 per cent is held by Canadian National Railways. The net proceeds from the sale of the government's Telesat shares will go to the debt servicing and reduction account. I understand that one of my colleagues in the opposition is asking the definition of net proceeds.
Basically net proceeds are all the money that is left over after the bills are paid. Telesat owes the Government of Canada $30 million. That is on our books and would have to be paid off by the moneys received from the proceeds of the sale, plus there are some legal expenditures and some finance expenditures for advisers on it, which are a minor part of the expenditures. But once those bills are paid, the entire balance goes into the debt reduction fund.
That is one of the things about our privatization program, as a matter of fact, that is different from other countries. For example, in Britain their Crown corporations are not on their books for anything. So every penny realized from a sale of a Crown corporation goes directly into their consolidated revenue fund. However, our situation in Canada is different. When Crown corporations are formed or borrow money from governments, they are put on the books of the government of the day and, of course, those loans, those moneys owing to the government must be repaid to the taxpayers of the

Government Orders
country when a sale takes place. Such as the case with Air Canada and such as the case here with Telesat.
The privatization program, I might point out, Mr. Speaker, also contributes to the growth of the Canadian economy. It does so by freeing up those commercially oriented Crown corporations whose potential for expansion and whose capacity to compete and diversify in an open market economy are stifled through the relative slowness of governmental decision making and through the lack of access to the equity capital markets for funds to help the company grow.
Since we began the privatization program, 20 privatization initiatives have been undertaken and nine entities have been dissolved. As a result of these initiatives, close to 50,000 employees have been transferred from the public to the private sector. In effect, the government's direct participation in the economy has been substantially reduced.

Telesat Canada was set up as a mixed enterprise, involving the government and several major communications carriers, with the mission to develop a national satellite telecommunications network. Today we can say: mission accomplished.

Telesat Canada now owns and operates six satellites, provides commercial satellite services and facilities nation-wide, including northern and remote areas of Canada. The company's revenues are derived from leasing satellite capacity to television broadcasting enterprises and telephone companies and through the provision of voice, data and imaging services to business. As well, the company offers international telecommunications consulting services.
In other words, Telesat Canada is a commercial success story and no longer requires government participation to fulfil its public policy role. In fact, continued government participation does not represent an appropriate use of taxpayers' dollars. Moreover, selling the government's Telesat shares will give the company both a stronger incentive and a more flexible means of pursuing its commercial opportunities.
Let me explain that in greater detail because I think it is very important for the people of Canada to understand. The company is subject to growing competition, most notably from domestic terrestrial carriers and Telesat's counterparts in the United States.
In order to compete successfully and retain its share of the market, Telesat must become more innovative, cost effective and efficient. That is why we are proposing to repeal the Telesat Canada Act and sell the government's Telesat shares to a private sector interest. Proceeding in this manner will enable Telesat to obtain access to the private equity capital and leadership that will help it to maintain its position in the marketplace and, of course, continue to provide state of the art services that users are demanding today.
Let me now turn to the key provisions of the legislation. The Telesat Canada reorganization and divestiture bill transfers the common shares of Telesat held by the Minister of Finance, 49.3 per cent as I mentioned earlier, to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization). It also transfers CN's 3.7 per cent interest in Telesat to the minister and as a result the minister of state will hold 53 per cent, a control block of the shares.
The legislation will authorize the minister to offer the majority block of Telesat shares for sale. CN will receive its proportionate share of the net proceeds from the sale of its shares. The net proceeds from the sale of the government's shares, as I mentioned earlier, will go the debt servicing and reduction account.
The bill also provides that the company be continued under the Canada Business Corporations Act. This will ensure that Telesat will be subject to the same corporate rules as other private business corporations. Upon continuance, the current Telesat Canada Act will be repealed.
I wish to emphasize to my hon. colleagues that under this legislation, no more than 20 per cent of Telesat shares may be owned in total, directly or indirectly, by non-residents of Canada. This will ensure that Telesat will remain Canadian controlled in the future while allowing a reasonable amount of foreign investment in the company. This provision conforms to the government's policy of restricting non-resident ownership in telecommunications carriers to the 20 per cent level.
November 19, 1991

The government has taken steps through this legislation to ensure that the company cannot be wound up without prior legislative approval. Telesat will also be required as a minimum to continue to establish satellite communications systems and provide satellite based telecommunication services in Canada. In this regard, the company will continue to be regulated as a telecommunications common carrier by the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission, the CRTC.
I briefly mentioned earlier that Telesat Canada provides commercial satellite services and facilities nationwide, including northern and remote areas of Canada. In fact, as a result of government policy, Telesat is the primary vehicle for providing the northern and remote areas of Canada with access to telephone, broadcasting and other telecommunications services which are so important for this vast country.
Accordingly, the government will require Telesat to continue to serve the northern and remote areas of Canada. I would stress that under the Radiocommunications Act, the government has the necessary legislative powers to enforce this policy, which I might add, should not increase Telesat's operating costs. In fact the provision of its services to the northern and remote areas of the country are profitable for Telesat and are unlikely to be abandoned under any scenario.
Returning to the legislation, as I stated, Telesat will continue to be regulated by the CRTC. As well, any transfer of control of Telesat will require prior approval of the CRTC. Similarly, Telesat will be restricted from selling, leasing, lending or otherwise disposing of its property which is integral to the provision of its key services again without the approval of the CRTC.
The CRTC believes that some of Telesat services are offered in sufficiently competitive markets and therefore these services need not be regulated. Therefore this bill gives the CRTC the power to refrain from regulating Telesat's activities where the CRTC is satisfied that the degree of market competition will ensure just and reasonable rates and non-discriminatoiy service.
Government Orders
Let me give you an example if I might. Satellite dishes are provided both by Telesat and by other many private suppliers. Therefore, the CRTC would not have to ensure the continued supply of these items. I think if any of us drive in any of our communities in any of our constituencies, we see a myriad of dishes of varying sizes and forms for sale. This needs not be regulated by the CRTC, so that of course is provided for in this bill.
It is not intended to circumvent CRTC's power to regulate Telesat-we should make that very clear-or in particular, the company's monopoly activities. I might say that this particular section in the bill is at the request of the CRTC. It feels that if there is competition in the marketplace, it should not be required to regulate one person or one individual supplier while the others are not being regulated. Of course that makes sense.
The government will also take steps to make sure that Telesat will be in an optimal position to supply its satellite services to Canadians. For a minimum of 10 years following the sale of the government's Telesat shares, no other telecommunications carrier will be issued a licence under the Radiocommunications Act to operate fixed satellite facilities in Canada.
This will contribute to a stable business environment for Telesat after the government has sold its shares in the company and is a reasonable approach, given expected traffic levels. It will also help Telesat to better serve the Canadian market and meet its responsibility of providing satellite based services to the northern and remote areas of Canada.
The government's privatization policy gives high priority to respecting the concerns of employees. The sale of the government's shares in Telesat will not affect the existing terms and conditions of employment, including employee pensions.
Also we will require as a condition of sale that the purchaser of Telesat continues the employee's share ownership plan that was implemented by the company in January 1990.1 might say in passing that over 60 per cent of the Telesat employees are participating in this plan. It has been very well received by the employees.

November 19, 1991
Government Orders
Bidders for the government's Telesat shares will also need to state their intentions regarding the use of Canada's two official languages and the maintenance of Telesat's headquarters and operations in the national capital region.
The government recognizes the importance of technology based industries to current and future economic development in Canada. Therefore, consistent with our desire that this important industrial sector continues to thrive, the agreement of purchase and sale will require Telesat to consider Canadian suppliers first and that the Minister of Communications be consulted about any major procurement plans of Telesat.
The divestiture of Telesat will proceed by way of a third party sale which will take place through a competitive bidding process. This will be put into motion following the passage of this bill.
As is standard there will be a first round to identify a short list of serious bidders. That would be followed by a final bidding from which the purchaser will be selected. With the exception of the 20 per cent non-resident ownership limit, there will be no restrictions on who may bid to purchase the government's shares in Telesat Canada. However, consistent with the government's policy of fostering competition within the telecommunications sector, the sale will be subject to the Competition Act.
What this means is that the sale will be reviewed by the director of investigation and research within the Bureau of Competition Policy to ensure that it complies with Canadian competition laws. The sale process will not commence until this bill receives royal assent. To facilitate that process I want to take this opportunity to encourage all interested parties to notify the director at the earliest opportunity of their intention to bid for our shares in Telesat. This will enable the director to identify at an early stage if there are competition issues that need to be addressed. I understand that already the director has been approached by companies interested in bidding.
I would encourage others that have not done so to do so.
Our approach to government ownership is pragmatic. We are not divesting ourselves of government holdings because of any ideological biases. Instead we are seeking
to rationalize government by divesting those Crown investments where government ownership is no longer necessary to fulfil a public policy purpose and by liberating commercially oriented Crown holdings with an economic potential that is unattainable as long as they remain under public stewardship.
In this respect the sale of the government's shares in Telesat will fully privatize the company. No longer will government officials and nominees sit on its board and no longer will it have to operate within the restrictions of the Telesat Canada Act.
This new freedom to manage its affairs in a fully commercial manner will allow Telesat to exploit fully the exciting opportunities in the rapidly changing telecommunications industry. Anybody who has had the pleasure of visiting the company's headquarters here in the national capital region will be very impressed at the technology that has been developed here in Canada and that is continuing to be developed. I know the member who represents the area where the company is located is in the House today and is very interested in this debate. He is nodding his head in agreement that it is a very exciting place to see. I do not want to start company tours out there or anything, but if people are interested I would certainly recommend that they visit because it is quite an exciting operation.
Finally I would say that a fully privatized Telesat should be able to capitalize on potential new business possibilities with its new owners. I think that goes without saying.
I look forward to the participation of opposition party colleagues in this debate and the ensuing study in committee. I believe that once carefully examined, all parties will see the wisdom of this divestiture, wholeheartedly support this bill and assure its passage in a reasonable period of time.

subtopic: TELESAT CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to address the second reading debate of the Telesat Canada bill. I have listened very carefully to the remarks of the hon. minister. During my remarks I will raise questions with regard to some of the issues he has discussed. I look forward to being able to deal with many of those issues later at committee.
November 19, 1991

Just what are we doing here now with this bill to privatize Telesat Canada? What is privatization these days?
The field of privatization has actually been around for quite a while. A long time before I got here I think it used to be called divestiture but that was not as nice a word as modern days demanded. At some point we developed the term privatization to take the place of the word divestiture. That coasted along for a little while. Then there was some thought that the word privatization was a little too narrow in focus and that perhaps the word private was not quite right and we developed the term public participation. I guess the term public participation sounded much more appealing to the public and it had a nice ring to it. Some of the other privatization bills that we have been through in this House have used the term public participation.
In this particular bill involving Telesat we do not use the term public participation. We use the term disposal. We may have gone full circle. We are now getting rid of something. The term is not quite so glamorous as the others, but we have to get on with the issue no matter what term we use.
Telesat Canada was founded in 1969 as has been pointed out. I want to bring the attention of the House to the objects that were put in place for Telesat Canada when it was founded. This is a statute of Canada so I suppose I do not have to read on and on. It is fairly short. The objects are to:
(a)	establish satellite telecommunication systems providing on a commercial basis telecommunication services between locations in Canada and, subject to the appropriate intergovernmental arrangements, to and between other locations;
(b)	supply, on a commercial basis, satellite telecommunication systems and elements thereof in Canada or elsewhere; and
(c)	provide, on a commercial basis, services associated with development, implementation and operation of satellite telecommunication systems and elements thereof in Canada or elsewhere.
I point out the words "or elsewhere" in subsections (b) and (c). Today I gather that Telesat has confined its telecommunications service deliveries to Canada or at least for the Canadian market. But there is another
Government Orders
Canadian company that is operating outside Canada carrying Canadian telecommunications internationally.
There is also a section here that requires Telesat Canada to utilize to the extent practicable Canadian research, design, industrial personnel technology and facilities and research and development connected with satellite telecommunication systems. That is quite a mandate. Since 1969 Canada has fostered a lot of development and progress in that field. I think it is fair to say that we have been on the leading edge as a country.
Telesat Canada now maintains six satellites in space. One other satellite was recently leased to an American multinational. It will be going out of service I gather in a relatively short period of time. All of these satellites that are up there will in fact end their useful lives either because of the bum out of the power source or the change in the orbit.
In any event our Anik satellites are doing well now and Telesat Canada is doing well now. Just for the record I would like to make sure that we know what kinds of dollars we are dealing with here. I have three or four useful statistics for reference here. The operating revenues for the last completed report for the financial year 1990 were $177.8 million. The net earnings, which is a simple term for the profit but is not exclusively profit, were $30.4 million. The shareholders' equity, which would be the book value of what the government says the operational entity is worth for all shareholders including the government, is $282.4 million. The equity per common share is $38.45 per share.
The point to be made in looking at all of these statistics and looking back over a few years is that Telesat has prospered. Telesat has done extremely well. It has roughly doubled in its revenue generation in the last five years and it appears to have a strong future in the field.
The government says that it is privatizing or disposing of Telesat for a number of reasons. One of them is that the government has said it has achieved its objectives. I think the minister has probably reiterated that here today. In the documentation accompanying the government's bill is a statement that the government has achieved its objective of encouraging introduction development and the use of satellites in space technology in

November 19, 1991
Government Orders
the domestic commercial telecommunication sector through its investment in Telesat.
Yes, it has achieved all of those objectives and is continuing to achieve those. But are those the only objectives that Telesat had? In my view there were objectives that went beyond that. It included having a strong government presence in a field where there was previously not enough activity.
Now the government claims to have achieved the domestic objective but surely the challenge of maintaining a strong, vital Canadian presence in this satellite telecommunications sector domestically, if not internationally, remains. Just because we have achieved the initial objective of having a strong presence does not mean the challenge does not continue.
I want to point out that in terms of the business of government, privatization on its own is not stable ground for fostering further government activity. It really does not get any easier in government than selling something. All one must do is bundle it together in a package, as through the Telesat annual report, and sell it. You have the proceeds and everyone thinks you have done a great job. What you are selling is the work of Canadians, the initiative of Canadians, the product of this Parliament and the taxpayers' resources. If it is going to be sold then we want value for our money, but I do not think it is safe to base a privatization simply on ideology.
Sometimes I think that the government listens too intently to some of its friends on the issue of ideology. If we are going to sell a government entity then it should be done for reasons other than simple ideology. It should be done for reasons that are viable in business and based on common sense.
I would note that to sell something purely for ideological reasons is just as bad or dumb as acquiring something for ideological reasons. This was the case with many nationalizations all over the world over the last 50 or 100 years. I do not think ideology has a great role to play in any business enterprise.
The government has stated here that its goal is a healthy market driven telecommunications sector. Now I am curious whether or not the mere fact of this sale by itself will generate this market telecommunications sector. We in this House are going to have to be the judge.
We are going to have to judge it in advance because after the entity is sold it is too late.
Telesat Canada has been a monopoly for 22 years and the government has committed to maintaining Telesat as a monopoly for a further 10 years. There is no disrespect intended with respect to the prospective purchasers of these shares in terms of their market orientation. But I want to ask a question. If it is a monopoly now and if it is to continue to be a monopoly for a further 10 years, how much more market driven will this telecommunications sector be than it is now? It is simply a monopoly. The marketplace that purchases the services of Telesat is market driven to be sure, but the monopoly service that is provided is simply a monopoly.
We are just at the time when we know we are entering a domain of global competition. We are just at a time when Canada's industrial sector including the telecommunications sector needs all the help it can get. We need all the government support we can muster to challenge the world. Just at that point in time the government has chosen to bail out of Telesat. I do not know whether the timing is good. I suggest that it may not be. Just when we have to devote all that we possibly can as a nation to making our globally competitive enterprises successful, we are going to unhitch Telesat from our train. It does not mean that Telesat cannot continue doing its commercial work.
I want to raise a question and it is a question we will be dealing with later in debate, I am sure. I wonder whether or not there is more out there for Telesat with government involved.
I want to raise two or three issues with respect to the mechanism of the disposal of the privatization. The minister has discussed for us the issue of section 5(3) net sale proceeds. I have read that several times and I have discussed it with others. The minister has made an attempt to describe how the sale proceeds will be dealt with here. I am not too sure I have it nailed down yet. If the minister is correct, and I am sure he is, then I have another question to follow that as we chase each other around in this shell game. There is a lot of money involved here. He mentioned a figure of $30 million as being what is on the books of the Government of Canada as a loan.
November 19, 1991

Consider that I had an automobile and I turned that over to an agent and said: "Sell my car". If I bought the car for $5,000 and I made some improvements on it and it was to be sold for $10,000, when the sale was over I would expect to have $10,000 in my pocket. This would be minus the sale expenses. There would be a few sale expenses. There always are. I think that agent would come to me and say: "Here is the $10,000 minus the $500 it cost to sell it". I would say: "Thank you very much. Now I am going to use the money. It is mine, that $9,500".
What the government has said here in section 5(3) of the act is that when this sale is over it is only going to put toward the debt and debt service the net sale proceeds over and above the book value. If the book value is $30 million that is fine. At the end of the day the government is going to get all of the money including the $30 million. The loan that it says is on its books and the money that was extended came out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund many years ago. That was taxpayers' money. I am sure it sits on government books as a loan, but it is an asset of the taxpayer just as the shares of Telesat are an asset of the taxpayer. I do not care whether the money coming back to the government is by the repayment of a loan or by the sale of the shares. All I know is that as a taxpayer I want to see all of the money put toward debt service and debt reduction as the government has said it would.
We need an explanation. If the loose change here or the book value is $30 million, we on this side of the House want to know what happens to that $30 million. I think it ought to go to paying down the debt and/or for debt service.
Another issue raised in the sale is the reference to referring this sale to the competition branch. That sounds pretty good, but I think it may be a red herring. I think it is window dressing. I think it is something that has been inserted into the bill to make the bill look stronger, fairer and better than it really is. I will try and explain why.
The reason why this sale is to be submitted for review under the Competition Act is to determine whether or not there would be "any lessening of competition as a result of the sale". We know that Telesat has had a monopoly for 22 years and we know that it is going to continue to have a monopoly for a further 10 years. I
Government Orders
cannot figure out how there could ever be any less competition anyway if it is going to continue as a monopoly.
It would be philosophically and logically impossible for the merger review branch under the Competition Act to find that there would be less competition. There is not any now and there will not be any. I guess what I am trying to say is a zero is a zero is a zero.
There may be elements surrounding telecommunications services that involve competition. In the downstream marketing of the service there may be some aspect of competition there that needs to be studied. We will be able to address that later in our committee review of this bill.
The third item involves section 14 in what we are now calling forbearance. Forbearance is a term generated in the not too distant past to describe the ability of administrative regulators to avoid or forbear or decline to regulate or exercise regulatory powers in a particular area. I gather that the Supreme Court of Canada has indicated that forbearance as a form of deregulation would be acceptable in the legal framework in Canada.
I do not have any problem with what they are saying, but I am sure all members would agree that if the government and/or this Parliament decides that there will or will not be a regulatory framework put in place for good public policy reasons then it should be this Parliament that makes the decision about whether or not the regulatory process should continue. I am not too sure that we want to be allowing the regulators to decide whether or not there should be regulation.
In this particular case and in fairness the government has indicated the criterion on which the regulator can base his decision on whether or not it will continue to regulate, and that means that criterion is the criterion of existing competition. This is the first time I have had to look at this mechanism of forbearance. I will call it back door deregulation. Before we implement it in this House I think we ought to make very sure it is exactly what we want.
Once it is put in place, and should problems develop in the field, Canadians could come back and say: "Wait a minute. We do not like what is happening there". We would have adopted a mechanism and put beyond our

November 19, 1991
Government Orders
reach at least for a short period of time the public policy regulatory initiative that is in place now.
The government has indicated that after the sale of Telesat it will continue the monopoly that it has now on a public policy basis. In other words, Telesat has the only gain in the satellite business for Canadian domestic telecommunications.
That is not in the bill. It is in the former statute. It is in the 1969 statute that created Telesat. It is not in the disposal of Telesat statute. I am not too sure why it is not there. If it is the government's policy to maintain a monopoly and continue a monopoly that existed in statute because it was put there by the legislators, I do not know why the government would not state that the monopoly would continue for another 10 years or for at least another 10 years.
In any event it is not there in the bill. The bill presumes that the public has made a decision or that this House has made a decision that a monopoly in providing these services is no longer necessary. I certainly have not come to that conclusion. There was a recent study commissioned by the government which discussed the issue of monopoly in telecommunication services. It referred to a period of a further five years. However that is an issue that my colleagues and I want to look more closely at before we are comfortable with all the provisions of this bill.
I want to raise a question in relation to the future of Telesat. It is really just conjecture, but we must recall that the only reason Telesat is there now is because there was a joint venture between the government and the private sector in 1969 or thereabouts. That is why it is there. Those are its roots and that is why it is thriving with its monopoly.
I can only speculate but I am curious about what will happen when the hardware that is up there now is finished. The satellites all have a useful life. I do not think any of them go beyond 10 years. I think eight years is one figure I read for the two current Anik-E satellites that were recently launched.
What happens when their orbits deteriorate or when they burn out? Will there be sufficient entrepreneurial initiative, with Telesat or whatever, to put up more Canadian satellites? I do not know that. There was not in 1969.
I know that the people who manage and run and give life to Telesat are professionals and business people. There are investors who have capital at stake. They are all large players such as Bell Canada, Telecom. There are some other investors as well.
Will there be the entrepreneurial initiative at that time to put up new satellites once the satellites have all gone their way? I do not have an answer to that, but I do know that there may well be competition which is not a bad thing. It is probably a good thing but the competition will be intense. It will come from countries like France, Japan and the United States as well as other countries whose governments continue to play a working role in telecommunications and in the business organization of space. I am not so sure that Canada ought to be pulling out. I have already made this point. I ask the question which we can continue to debate, and we will certainly ask the question at committee.
A fourth item related to the process of the sale is the commitment by the government to ensure the fostering of Canadian technology after the sale. It has described its commitment two separate ways in the documentation accompanying the bill. There is absolutely no reference to fostering Canadian technology in the bill itself.
Having pointed that out, I also want to recall for the House, because I have read it into the record, that the initial Telesat Canada bill did precisely that. It mandated the corporation to foster Canadian technology and information in that field. The first statement is that the government will require first consideration be given to Canadian suppliers. The other statement is that Telesat will have to use best efforts to buy from Canadian suppliers.
Maybe I am being too technical but first consideration and best efforts are two different mechanisms, two different standards. When those two different standards are held out in a framework where there is no statutory mandate, no requirement at all, I am curious exactly what Telesat is going to be asked to do.
Telesat will be composed of business people who will want to go out and cut good deals for their corporation. That is what their job is. That is what they are going to do. I am sure that they will not want to have their hands tied all the time in the way they make their purchases. They will want to buy good components and good information for good prices.
November 19, 1991

If the government is saying to us that it will insist that Telesat do this and if it is telling us by two different means what it wants, then the message when it is finally put to Telesat is going to be fuzzy. I think we would want to nail down that standard.
I would prefer to see something in the bill itself. As it stands now I think we can all acknowledge that what is there now in terms of commitment is not a promise. It really is not a commitment. It is a wish by the government that Telesat do that. I think that Canadians may want Telesat to do more than just want to buy Canadian or want to foster. I think we want to make sure that this area of telecommunications, where we are involved in the leading edge, is one that we remain strong in globally.
The last item has to do with access to the information after the sale. The government is going to make a decision about the bidding process. This is going to be a bidding process for these shares. It will not be a sale to the public through a stock market or through brokers. It will in fact be a process involving bids by parties that want to buy all or a part of the portion of Telesat that is for sale, slightly more than 53 per cent.
For those of us in this House who care about what happens to the taxpayers' dollars, and I know we all do, I know that when the sale is over we want to see where the money came in and where it went after that. We want to know how much was paid and if there was cash or something else as consideration.
We want to know what the other consideration for the purchase was. If it is as simple as cash that is great; it is easier to count. The Auditor General is very good at counting. The only issue then is the one I raised earlier involving the disposition of those moneys, which are now counted as being book values for the government.
I note that after the sale of de Havilland aircraft to Boeing we in this House have not to date been given all of the financial details. The sale was accomplished by means of a Governor in Council order, that is a statutory instrument. It is in fact a law of Canada.
I want to point out that I sit on a committee that has asked for that statutory instrument, that Order in Council, and the government has said that we cannot have it. We cannot have it because it was passed in cabinet. That
Government Orders
is a very serious problem. That is part of another agenda in another part of Parliament and is ongoing. However I do not think it is right. I know it is wrong for a government to sell an asset and when the legislators, the parliamentarians, ask what the terms of the deal were, how the money was moved around, the government says it is sorry but it cannot tell us.
There may be elements of commercial confidentiality involved in some of these transactions. Surely the government can find a way to deal with the commercial confidentiality. Members of this House certainly will want to do that. As I say that is another issue. But as we proceed with this privatization I rhetorically ask a question. When the financial details of this sale are complete six months or a year from now, if some member or a committee of this House asks what happened in this sale, where did the money go, how was it moved around, what were the terms, is the government going to say it is sorry but it cannot tell us? I hope not.
The record is not good. There are other issues like cabinet confidentiality that have to be taken into account here. I know this is going to be dealt with later. I raise it now so that as the minister prepares for whatever happens in cabinet he will take into account the fact that the members of this House are going to want to know what happened. It is only a matter of time before the question is asked.
I want to conclude. I began by discussing the role of ideology in some of the areas of privatization, not just in Canada but around the world. Eastern Europe is one area where there is a lot of privatizing going on. But there is privatizing going on even in communist states such as the Peoples Republic of China. It is helping to generate increased economic activity, market driven economic activity, where previously there was virtually none if we exclude the black market.
We have accomplished a great deal in this country, in North America and around the world, through ongoing government participation in large enterprises. Our world did not put men in space; the private sector did that. In every case man's space exploration involved a government commitment and participation. That happened in the U.S.A. That happened in the U.S.S.R. That happens in France now. Every single initiative has a government relationship behind it, and pardon the pun but that is what made it fly.

I do not think we should ever lose sight of the fact that government involvement in a mixed economy, in entrepreneurial initiatives, is not a bad thing.
I cannot wait to see the great rush of politicians to address and support the proposed high speed train from Quebec to Windsor in that corridor. I know it is a sleeper out there. I think there will be some proposals coming forward, but I will bet dollars to doughnuts there will be a mile long of politicians ready to jump in and pitch a piece of that high speed train technology and the enterprise. We have a mixed economy and we have to recognize it.
This government has a role to play in fostering all Canadian enterprise directly and indirectly, through involvement and non-involvement. It has to get on with it and knows it.
In terms of our general support for this bill, I have already raised a number of questions we believe are significant. We are in a position where we cannot support the bill at this time. subtopic: TELESAT CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is good to have the opportunity to address this particular telecommunications issue.
I want to say first off, speaking on behalf of my New Democratic colleagues, that we have not taken an ideological approach in determining our support or lack of support for this particular piece of legislation. We look at it in terms of a pragmatic policy framework with respect to the issues of whether or not it makes sense in terms of cost recovery, in terms of the consumers' interests, and with respect to the development of future public policy initiatives.
In some aspects the privatization of Telesat may provide some benefits. I know, for example, right now that the industry is in deep difficulty with respect to the financial resources that can be set aside for research and development. Not much is going on there. It simply does not have the capacity to do so. A privatized industry may free up some of the initiatives to assist in that and I recognize that. But I think we have to look at it in
addressing whether or not this process of privatization, be it good or bad, is in fact appropriate for today.
I want to present three reasons why I think Telesat Canada should not be privatized, at least not at this time. First of all, in Canada we have a telecommunications policy that is virtually non-existent. We are sadly lacking in terms of an updated policy framework that we can take some philosophic direction from with respect to the whole question of whether or not this industry should be deregulated, privatized, et cetera. We really do not have that policy framework in place. Without this policy framework, this direction, we cannot really tell whether the privatization of Telesat Canada is in fact going to be in the long run beneficial or detrimental to Canada's interests.
Second, I want to address some of the financial aspects of this privatization. Telesat today is not in as attractive a position as it was a couple of years ago for the process of privatization to take place. Today it has a very high debt capital ratio. Without higher rates, which it has not been able to obtain through the CRTC, it is projected that Telesat Canada is going to lose money over the next few years.
It does not look good in terms of market opportunity for the disposal of these Crown assets, the 53 per cent controlling interest that Canada has in Telesat. I want to go into that in more detail.
The third point is the fact that Telesat Canada is this country's only domestic satellite telecommunication system for broadcasting, data and telephone transmission. The question remains that because it is our only domestic system, should Canada with a vested interest in this corporate entity be relinquishing its controlling interest? I think that is a very pertinent question to ask.
I want to return in more detail to each of these points that I have made. I want to touch first upon the lack of a definitive telecommunications polity in Canada. As I mentioned there is currently no federal policy on telecommunications, and yet the government is proceeding on an almost ad hoc basis through its process of privatization. One would think it is being driven by an ideological approach to try to sell off as many Crown assets as possible. There is no federal policy in telecommunica-

tions and yet we are going to sell off this very vital and important asset.
It is our satellite link to northern and remote areas of this country. It allows Canadians to see themselves through their own eyes. I have some serious reservations as to whether or not we should be relinquishing our window of opportunity in that industry.
Areas of Canada north of the 55th parallel depend almost entirely on satellite telecommunications for receiving long distance signals. Telesat carries virtually all the regional, interprovincial and national radio and television in Canada for our northern and more isolated communities. Eldon Thompson, president of Telesat Canada, said recently: "Given the sparse population of our country and our very difficult terrain and sometimes hostile climate, the Canadian telecommunications system has become vital to both the economic and social affairs of our country and our citizens". I think that everybody would agree with that statement. It is a very appropriate one. That is what makes the whole question of whether or not we should be relinquishing our control of this industry even more vital.
It said in the press release that it is the policy of the federal government that Telesat will be "required to follow the current government policy of providing the northern and remote areas of Canada with access to telephone, broadcasting and other communications services". That is not in the bill. I find the lack of this specific initiative, the fact that it is not in the bill, to be quite troublesome.
Policy is set by the government of the day. Policy can be changed easily as governments are changed. The question is: What guarantee do our northern and isolated communities have that the policy will not change? Without the benefit of an active Parliament, northern and remote areas could in fact lose their essential satellite services. This is reflected in Mr. Thompson's statement that I have just quoted. It is not in the bill. It is a sad oversight that the bill does not in fact entrench this requirement.
Although the Minister of Communications has said there is no special cost in providing service to northern and remote areas, no one really knows what the lay of the land is going to be in terms of our technological
Government Orders
future, even five or six years from now. Will that have an effect on our ability to provide this northern and remote service?
I would like to quote what the president of Telesat said just recently in committee hearings. He was reflecting on the fact that in 1997 the company may not be making money. He was talking about replacements for the hardware, the satellites, and said:
When we get to 1997 and we have to commission replacements for them, the shareholders may decide they cannot afford them or they will build something very small to carry voice and data traffic for the north only.
I think that outlines a very legitimate concern. The cash flow projections for Telesat over the next decade are not terribly healthy. What happens when they have to commission the cost of a new satellite and they do not have the operating funds to do so? What happens when there is no statutory requirement through this current legislation to entrench the necessity for the provision of northern remote services? It may very well be sacrificed or trimmed down quite significantly.
Does this mean that the north and remote areas of Canada, which are the bulk of the land mass of Canada, may only have assured service over the next decade?
The other point I want to make in this respect is that policies that have been directing our broadcast system have been made almost on an ad hoc basis. There is really no contemporary social policy framework in which to set the direction for telecommunications in Canada. Policies that direct our broadcast system have been made by looking through a microscope. Policies have been made to fit each individual area, with no over-all regulatory framework.
The technology of today has far outpaced the regulatory framework in which we continue to operate. I mean our federal policy is really embodied in an act which is almost 60 years old now. It is called the Railway Act from when we were dealing with telegraphy in Canada. Good heavens, we now have digitalization of services. We have direct broadcast satellites. We have short wave. We have the advent of optical fibre networks. None of this is addressed in that legislation. We have no capacity in our current legislative framework to deal with these advances that are taking place at an accelerating rate.
We have no policy to deal with the American death stars which are really direct broadcast satellites and will

November 19, 1991
5. ft 31
have a major impact on our broadcasting system. These kinds of questions simply have not been addressed because of that lack of policy framework. Yet here we go, ready to sell off one of our very important and very crucial assets in terms of a window in the telecommunications industry.
We are preparing to enter the 21st century with policies and regulations that are mired in the stone age of technology. I guess that is the simplest way to put it.
I see my time is limited. I hope I will have the opportunity to continue the debate after the House breaks. In that regard the sale of Telesat is premature. It is akin to putting the technological cart before the policy horse. The current system in that respect does not serve public or corporate interests. It is inefficient for telecommunications companies to explore avenues, do the research and development that is necessary and apply to the CRTC to find that their efforts were wasted because that may not in fact be the direction that the CRTC wants them to move.
My argument here is that before we do anything we have to update our policy. We have to update the direction in which Canada wants to go in terms of whether or not our telecommunications carriers should be privatized and whether or not they should continue to be regulated or in fact deregulated.
With respect to profitability I want to come back to this second point. I mentioned earlier that Telesat Canada is in a precarious financial position. Because of that I submit that its future very much depends on the agenda that will be set by its future shareholders, whoever those shareholders may be.
Telesat's shares were purchased in 1969 for some $30 million. Since then it has brought in almost $22 million in cash dividends over the years. It is not really costing the Canadian taxpayer any money. That money was invested at that time and is sitting there. Cash dividends have been returned to the Crown through the years and, if my numbers are correct, that $30 million translated into 1991 dollars would actually be worth almost $120 million.
We do have a substantial investment in there. I see my time is up. I will continue with this discussion at the earliest opportunity.

Mr. Speaker, the recent breakdown of the unity committee is an example of Canadian politics at its very worst.
In no other sector of Canadian society would a committee collapse into ultimatums and boycotts because there were differences in the organization or operation; not a town council, not a business boardroom, not a church committee, not any committee. Regular people would discuss the problems, resolve them and carry on. They do it every day. But here partisan politics takes over and the interests of politicians take priority over the interests of the country and everything else.
Probably all parties involved have made mistakes, including the Conservatives, the NDP and the Liberals. It is time they got on with the purpose of the committee and did the job they were sent here to do.
It is interesting to me that not one of my constituents has asked a question or even made a comment about the unity committee. Perhaps they just consider it more proof that we politicians are up here in an ivory tower dealing with problems we want to deal with but not the problems they want to deal with.

Mr. Speaker, today in Washington, D.C. The Black Canoe, the Spirit of Haida Gwaii, will be officially dedicated at the Canadian embassy. This masterpiece of monumental art perfectly distils the history, mood, desire, spirit and hope of the Haida people and humanity.

noon to tell my children the story of this black canoe and its 13 occupants. The stories of dogfish woman, bear mother, wolf, raven and the ancient reluctant conscript had a permanent effect on their lives.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to announce that in Geneva today Canada, along with the United States and most European countries, signed a major international protocol which calls for measures to reduce emissions of pollutants which cause smog.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, Canada has played a lead role in shaping this protocol and in promoting the needs and targets of specific geographic areas for emission reductions.
The protocol is designed to reduce emissions of volatile organic compounds, VOCs, a major cause of ground level ozone, the major component of smog. This protocol will permit Canada to achieve a 30 per cent reduction of VOC emissions by 1999 in the lower Fraser Valley and in the Windsor-Quebec corridor.
The protocol also commits Canada to a national freeze of VOC emissions at 1988 levels to be achieved by 1999.
This represents a significant commitment and will require major efforts on the part of government, industry and the Canadian public, all of whom have participated in the development of the federal-provincial NOX/VOC management plan to reduce smog.

subtopic: TELESAT CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I was saying before the debate was temporarily interrupted, one of the difficulties that we face with regard to the disposal of assets of Telesat is the fact that right now it is undergoing some financial duress.
It is really not an appropriate time to be divesting the public shares of Telesat. The company has a debt load that quite frankly would choke a horse. The poor financial outlook of Telesat is expected to extend into the next decade as a result of recent heavy capitalization and a burdensome rate structure which has been imposed on it by the CRTC.
The corporation has a debt capitalization ratio of over 60 per cent which is pretty significant. That 1990 figure is almost double the ratio for 1987. Its cash flow to debt financing has grown considerably weaker since 1986. During the next two fiscal years the corporation faces considerable escalation of its debt repayment schedule.
I might add much of the current financial woes really stem from a CRTC decision which has allowed for an annual rate increase of a modest 2.67 per cent.
This decision disallowed the inclusion of what I consider to be significant expenses in the calculation of the rates adopted and what Telesat officials believed to be an overly optimistic view of the market. It has a real cash flow crunch.

Government Orders
As a result the company has been thrust into an extremely low earnings position. It is not expected to achieve allowable earnings for several years. I found this in my discussions with the representatives at Telesat.
Corporate profitability will therefore become increasingly difficult during the early years of operation of its new series of satellites. Eldon Thompson is the CEO of Telesat. I will quote him once again: "It will be extremely difficult if at all possible to operate and maintain long-term service. The rate decision exacerbates the inherent cyclical nature of the satellite business since it ensures that the lowest prices are charged at a time when the company's costs are the highest".
It is only natural in looking at the financial projections of Telesat to conclude that any investor who is looking at acquiring the shares of Telesat and looking at the cash flow projections and the debt to capital ratio is not going to be overwhelmed with the idea. I do not think the share offering can be expected to be too optimistic.
In other words, what I am saying is that it is not the appropriate time given the market circumstances for a kind of a fire sale giveaway because I think that may very well be what it amounts to. It is therefore unlikely that the sale, if it takes place at this time, would be of great financial benefit to the taxpayers of Canada in terms of cash recovery to the Crown.
As I said before there may be some reasons to look at privatization. I think the question is: Why now, particularly? I realize my time is limited. I only have a short time left. I will go on to summarize more or less my feelings on this whole thing. Canada's shareholdings in Telesat represent a considerable investment in the future of Canadian telecommunications.
The government wants to opt out of this investment at a time when we are experiencing essentially a worldwide revolution of technological change in the industry. For Canada to forfeit its shares and window of opportunity in our only space based telecommunications industry means that we would essentially be forgoing the opportunity to provide direction in terms of policy direction for this country at a very critical time in the evolution of this industry and in the evolution of that corporate entity.
In addition Canada has not yet fleshed out a well defined communications strategy. We have entered the 21st century of high-tech change cobbled with a policy that has evolved in the horse and buggy days of technological evolution.
I think it is a serious mistake to forfeit our investment in Telesat at this particular time and before we have delineated a comprehensive communications strategy.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to my colleague's speech.
There are a couple of points that I would like to make and then maybe I could ask him a question. He talked about cash flow, debt ratios, et cetera. He compared 1987 to 1990.
This particular business, the satellite business, is cyclical. The front end costs are tremendous. It has to hire a company that propels satellites into outer space. It has to buy these satellites and have them made. In this particular case it was made at Spar Aerospace at tremendous capital cost.
The first two or three years of the cycle is extremely expensive for the company. That is the cycle that we are in right now. Everyone held their breath in Canada for some time because the first satellite did not deploy exactly the way they wanted it to. They had to do what the experts refer to as a "shake and bake" to get it operating. But they did get it operating.
The second satellite has been launched successfully as well. There were tremendous up front costs. This company traditionally and any company involved in satellite telecommunications realizes their profits in the last half of the cycle. That is when they start making money. To say that we are selling it at the wrong time now is a fallacy because those who will be buying this company understand full well the cyclical nature of the major capital expenditures and at the same time the profit that comes at the other end.
With regard to Mr. Thompson's concerns about the CRTC's decisions on rates, naturally that is a concern, but as my hon. friend knows full well, the government has given orders to CRTC to review the rate schedule because of the inordinate costs up front. Again, those who would be purchasing this company will be very much aware of all of that and will be taking that into consider-

ation. I do not think that there is a problem there at all as to the timing of the sale.
My question is this. The hon. member is giving us the old socialist New Democratic line.

This company has asked to be privatized so that it can expand and it can take on the new challenges that are coming down the line. Of course, being a pragmatic government, we examined what their requests were and we said: "Sure, we are prepared to go along because it does not serve a public policy purpose".

Mr. Speaker, if you will recall, in my opening remarks I said that rather than an ideological approach to this whole question of privatization, there may be very sound reasons for going ahead with privatization. One of those reasons I cited in passing was the opportunity for more research and development to take place. That is a positive reason.
One of the arguments I put forward was the fact that we have to make this decision based upon some pragmatic objectives, the objective of rationalization cost recovery if we are in fact going to get the money back and we are going to maximize our return in terms of cash assets

to the Crown. I do not think we will at this particular time.
The second reason I gave, which the minister was not here to listen to, was the fact of consumer interest. What is in the long-term interest of the consumers of the services offered by Telesat?
Last, we are making this decision in the absence of well-defined and well-flushed out policy initiatives. I was arguing at that time, and I think the minister was back to hear the tail end of those arguments, that in fact we are putting the technological cart before the policy horse. We in fact do not have comprehensive policy to take us into the 21st century of technology change. We are mired in a kind of a horse and buggy day, the stone age of our technology. The Railway Act is the main legislation body that directs communications in Canada today. We need to bring our policy up to date to take account of all the technological change that has taken place to set us on a specific philosophical approach to this whole realm of telecommunications. Once we have that determined and are moving in the right direction then perhaps it makes sense to disperse the assets of Telesat. I am suggesting that we cannot make that decision until we take the time and develop the comprehensive policy that is needed to meet the needs of today. Then and only then can we really determine whether the sale of Telesat is in the interest of Canadians and this government.
