speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am really quite pleased to stand here this afternoon and participate at this stage of the debate on the principles of Bill C-138, this bill to privatize Telesat Canada.
There are some very serious questions about the government's decision to privatize Telesat at this time. They are all important enough questions. I would consider them to be principles of this privatization legislation. What are perceived to be policies are really fundamental principles in the Canadian dynamic.
Some on the government benches may well argue with the points I shall now raise, but I believe they have to be addressed in a most serious way in the best interest of Canada and the business community.
This bill is coming forward in a telecommunication policy vacuum. It fails to protect northern services and the monopoly status that Telesat presently enjoys. The reliance on the Competition Act through the Competi-

November 19, 1991
Government Orders
tion Bureau is not a good telecommunication policy method for screening bidders. There is a failure to question whether broadcasters should be able to bid, as well as the vague terms and conditions of sale. Add to that the terms of a Canadian procurement policy, the invitation rather than the obligation to use both official languages, the location of its headquarters, the lack of reason for rejecting a public share offering and the lack of a floor policy for bidding. These are all, I believe, critical issues.
I know the minister may have some quick answers to some of these questions and I look forward to getting some of these answers before this bill goes much further.
First and foremost we must recognize at the outset that Telesat is an important national asset. Canada must continue to be a major player in the satellite field if we are to benefit from new technologies, services, high-tech jobs and research and development spending which this company brings to Canada, Canadians and Canadian business.
In this era of fast changing technology this sector is the engine, the fulcrum, the economic lever which can enable, as well as ensure, our competitive capacity in this very competitive international environment.
Ensuring that Telesat remains a viable national asset for the benefit of all Canadians has to be uppermost in our minds. That should be a given for the policy makers across this floor. After all, it was the Canadian taxpayer that made the key investment that got this company off the ground in the first place some two decades ago.
Long before you get to the privatization question you have to make sure that you have established the appropriate policy environment, in this case telecommunications policy, before a privatization can even be considered. This is something the federal government has clearly failed to do. It has failed to establish any sort of national strategy for the telecommunications sector despite promises that date back to the era of the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre in the 1984 economic statement. I quote that statement to remind the government. Ele said: "There is a clear need for national
telecommunications policy to take advantage of the opportunities presented by rapidly advancing technology and the growing demand by Canadians for new telecommunications services".
He added: "Through regulatory reform the government can spur innovation and provide a major stimulus to the Canadian economy". Yet the telecommunications revolution is breaking every new record every day around us. It has moved forward at a rapid pace since 1984 that could never have been dreamed of. This government has left the Telecom industry labouring under the century-old Railway Act without updating rules and regulations for the era of global competition.
Telecommunications industry revenue has grown to more than $21 billion a year. It plays a role in the daily life of nearly every Canadian. Its impact on business has been phenomenal. Global capital markets now function because of global telecommunications. Companies large and small now communicate with customers, distant offices and employees at home through telecommunications. There are new telecommunication ads which I am sure you have seen, Mr. Speaker, such as the Bell Canada ad where the man is going on his vacation while the other man is rushing off to meet his counterparts in the industry around the country. They are busy talking about teleconferencing, which is also offered by Unitel and Telesat.
These are the realities of what is going on in the telecommunications world today. Digital technology is a reality as is fibre optics. The whole field of broadcasting, radio and television is testament to the changes that are taking place in telecommunication technology.
The Americans have built vast global networks and yet this federal government is left watching these dramatic changes in its rear view mirror. Now we have the Telesat privatization going on in this policy vacuum. Seven years ago the past Minister of Finance, the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre and the prior Minister of Communications, the hon. member for Frontenac, and even Flora MacDonald promised a bold new Telecom policy. Even the impartial observer would agree that this government's record has certainly not been very successful. This government has failed to update and revise a comprehensive national telecommunications policy or strategy which is the fundamental environment in which Telesat operates.
November 19, 1991

Government Orders
The policy vacuum and lack of national telecommunications strategy into which this government wants to sell Telesat are truly a major concern. Would you not agree with that?
Telesat is the only Canadian carrier providing commercial satellite facilities and services across this land. It is also the only Canadian carrier providing basic telecommunications services to the northern communities and to the remote regions of Canada. That is the second principle I want to debate with respect to this legislation.
Is this government going to leave them out there with no communication facilities that are protected? Why has this government seen fit to protect those very vital and very valuable northern services only through government policy? A cynic would say that such a policy is on very thin ice in the hands of this government. I would add that the official's argument that once a satellite is up there is no reason why anyone would stop providing services to the north is a highly questionable proposition to say the least. Don't you need receiving stations and earth stations? Don't they involve costs and require expensive maintenance? Don't they require expensive and regular adjustments? What about the cost of new investments in the latest technology to receive the satellite signals?
These items bring into doubt the government's urging not to worry about the continuation of northern services by Telesat once sold off. Once the satellites are up there they are basically free, according to this government. Hopefully we can be forgiven if we do not take the minister's word on this issue. This should be founded in the legislation, not left to the whim and will of the government in power.
I am anxious for the government to explain to those northern and remote communities how the proposal of a mere policy of service to their communities is worth much, if anything, particularly when it is subject to change at the whim of a minister. That I would suggest is not very reassuring, comforting or Canadian for that matter. Service to the north must be protected in the legislation and that is what we will be pushing for if this goes to legislative committee. Frankly it should just be put on a back-burner somewhere and be revisited.
I would also like to address the government's proposal to assure a 10-year monopoly for Telesat in the form of government policy, just as in the northern service. The question of a monopoly service has not been addressed and is to be left after privatization. That just makes no sense.
Yes, we need an entire debate about foreign competition, about market conditions, about Canadian content in service, and I could go on and on. Suffice it to say, the government has put the cart before the horse with this legislation. The lack of some clear, new thinking from the government on monopoly satellite services is another extremely large component of the policy vacuum that I talked about earlier.
For now I think the monopoly is important for Telesat so that it can remain a vital national asset and a national satellite service provider, given current market conditions. Obviously the government agrees or is at least paying lip service to the idea. It mentions that a policy of monopoly provider status will be established for Telesat once it is privatized. That is an irresponsible approach and it ducks the issue.
Again a cynic would ask: if the government believes so strongly in the monopoly provision, then why not put it in legislation? Only another cynic would suggest it is not assured in the bill so that if the government decided to drop the monopoly protection at the urging of the new owner it could be far more easily changed than a policy that is already in legislation.
There are some questions that I believe we shall have to ask. What are the real costs in terms of only having policy and not legislative protection of the monopoly? How do potential bidders see this affecting a privatized Telesat? And, more important, what are the costs to Canadian taxpayers of this uncertainty with regard to the monopoly status of Telesat and the real costs of this uncertainty in the form of lower bids for the company? These are some real questions we will want explored at legislative committee.
There are two issues with regard to the open bidding process. Why was a public share offering rejected? Why is the Competition Act being used to screen bidders, not a modern, updated, sound telecommunication policy for the 1990s?
First we would like to know-and it is a key principle of this bill-why the public share offering was rejected as an option in this proposed sale. Would not the taxpayers

November 19, 1991
Government Orders
then have had a chance to participate in Telesat Canada's success story?
Canadians have already paid as investors. Do you think we have conveniently forgotten that Canadian taxpayers' dollars are already involved in this particular story? Is the minister setting up Telesat for some big player to come in and grab it? Is the minister seeking out critical mass in some telecommunications industry segment by letting anyone bid? The point is that there is no evidence that these critical questions were even addressed by the government in deciding on a open bidding rather than other privatization methods. That is a very vital question we will want to have answered in committee.
Why is the Competition Act the only criterion being used for screening bidders for a key component of Canada's communication industry? I think that is an important question. The answer I think is that this government lacks a clear, cohesive and comprehensive national telecommunications strategy. We should have had a policy that was revised and updated, that knows and understands all the Telecom markets and players, domestic and international, in order to screen bidders fairly in a telecommunications policy context. To leave one of the key telecommunications issues in this decade, namely who gets hold of Telesat, exclusively to the determination of the Competition Bureau is a serious flaw not only by the privatization minister and the Minister of Communications but by the whole cabinet. Where is their responsibility in response to the people of Canada? What does it mean by allowing a group of bureaucrats who may be very competent but are nonetheless non-elected people make decisions as to how a bid is receivable and the nature of that bid? I thought we were supposed to be a government of elected representatives.
We should not have the spectacle of the competition bureau making telecommunication policy for Canada. We do here in this bill.
I wonder how our communications minister feels about the extent of his contribution on this matter appearing as a couple of paragraphs in the Minister of State for Privatization's press release. Do you think, Mr. Speaker, that made him feel very comfortable? Irony of ironies, it is just this past week that the Minister of Labour, doing the Minister of Communciation's work,
brought in the status of artist legislation. Now we have a Minister of State for Privatization bringing in communications policy'.
We now have communications and cultural policy by the privatization and the labour ministers, dictated by Treasury Board and determined by the Minister of Finance. Why do we have a Minister of Communications? It is a very good point that ought to be raised in the committee.
Does the Minister of Communications not feel a very sad loss of power? Does he not feel badly? If he does not he really should. He should go back to the cabinet and discuss this whole issue.
The telecommunications policy decision of who can bid for Telesat is key to this whole process, to the structure of this industry and to the industry's future development. Again, this is another question we will want to put before both ministers at legislative committee.
I think the Minister of Communications' abdication of policy responsibility on the Telesat privatization poses many more questions as well. Should Canadian broadcasters be able to bid and possibly own Telesat? Do you, Mr. Speaker, recall what we did in the broadcasting bill with respect to people who are in the telecommunications field with respect to a broadcast right?
I do not know the answers to these questions. I hope the ministers do. I do believe it is a matter of telecommunications and broadcasting policy, not competition policy. That is the mistake of the Minister of Communications and that is the mistake he allowed to happen in this bill.
Since when has this country, except up until now, allowed culture and communications policy to be made by bureaucrats in the Competition Bureau? I think this is really the wrong path to be going down and it is another issue that I would like to hear the two ministers discuss in committee.
It is pretty well toward the end of the questions I have about just how loose and freely this bidding process has been set up. Why are companies simply being invited to state their intentions with regard to how they would address Telesat's future operations in both official languages? Why is this not being made a condition of the bid, a real demand on the bidders?
November 19, 1991

I see the privatization minister's cynical hands over all these wishy-washy vague requests for comment on how official languages would be maintained by suitors of Telesat. It is insufficient. It is not good enough and that is another issue to be pursued. Has this minister heard of the Official Languages Act of Canada? Does he know that federally regulated organizations fall under that Official Languages Act? Is that why he wants to know whether he is going to keep Telesat as a monopoly service and all the other things that he is going to do in terms of regulation?
Again, there is the question of the minister's weak demand on the part of bidders for where they will locate Telesat. He says that bidders will be asked to state their intentions regarding Telesat's headquarters in the national capital region and the government will choose a winning bidder not based in part on this information but simply in full knowledge of the bidder's plans.
I see this as just another weak way of passing off key issues related to privatization. I find the terms and conditions provisions of the procurement rules to be followed by Telesat bidders also inadequate. Why should Telesat bidders be only asked to consider Canadian supplier proposals and to use best efforts to buy Canadian?
Was Canadian procurement not a key reason why we set up Telesat, to get a domestic industry off the ground? Was it not a key reason why we set up Telesat and why we have Spar Aerospace today?
Finally, Mr. Speaker, and I note that I have less than one minute left, I wonder why the government has not provided for the public record any evaluations on what it deems Telesat to be worth.
Why cannot Canadians have the privilege of knowing what the value of their shares in Telesat are worth before the privatization minister gets his hands on the bids so that taxpayers and not just the minister can get to see what kind of dollars we are talking about.
I wonder why the minister did not set a floor price for the Telesat shares on behalf of all taxpayers. Would that not have been in the best interests of both the taxpayers and the minister, seeing that he is claiming that he will

put the proceeds from this sale in that paper tiger, the deficit reduction fund.

the government, in an effort to strengthen the implications and the intent of the Official Languages Act, is in fact requiring the bidders to state their intentions with respect to that matter.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by congratulating the hon. member for Mount Royal on her excellent presentation on the Telesat Canada bill.

I wonder if the member shares my concern. I am sure she must and if she could comment concerning access to information after sale.
Fifty-three per cent of Telesat Canada shares are owned by the Canadian government with a possible worth of $150 million plus. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to rise today and take the opportunity to speak on Bill C-38, an act to provide for the privatization of Telesat Canada.
Government Orders
Once again we are faced with legislation that comes as a result of this government's philosophical obsession to diminish the ability of the Government of Canada to make policies in areas of national importance and regional significance.
I have some concerns about this legislation that I want to outline. First I want to take a few minutes and talk about the desire the government seems to have to want to privatize practically everything.
Canadians have seen their train service severely diminished through cuts to VIA Rail. The privatization of Air Canada has jeopardized the services that are required in the north and other regions of our country.
At the present time the process is under way of cutting off our ability to influence the ever important national resource industry through the commencement of the privatization of Petro-Canada.
This government literally brags about the profits that the privatized Canada Post has produced in recent times while ignoring the fact that post offices have been closed throughout rural Canada. This has in some cases severely damaged the character of rural communities. It has caused a great deal of concern among rural Canadians who are fighting to keep their towns, villages and communities alive.
Now we have this government putting forward legislation which again could take the hand of the Canadian people out of the satellite communications field. Once again we have to very closely scrutinize the government's plan in a very thorough manner to ensure that this legislation is in the best interests of Canadian people, rather that just another example of this government's right wing Conservative philosophy.
We must also examine this legislation to ensure that it is written in a way that the interests of Canadians are paramount, rather than the special individuals or private investors or corporate players.
Telesat was founded or established under the Trudeau Liberal government in 1969 by the Telesat Canada Act. It was a joint venture between the government and the major communication carriers to develop a domestic commercial satellite based telecommunications system.

November 19, 1991
Government Orders
It is the only Canadian carrier providing commercial satellite services and facilities across Canada.
There are other concerns that I want to raise about this legislation. For many Canadians, in particular those living in the north and remote areas of Canada, the satellite services provided by Telesat Canada are perhaps the only practical and affordable means of providing broadcasting, telephone and other telecommunication services.
I was informed a while ago that Telesat Canada will continue to provide these satellite services for the provision of telecommunication services to northern and remote areas. When I heard that, I was certainly relieved. But as I read through this legislation I find to my surprise and alarm that there is no mention of maintaining these essential satellite services to the north and remote areas. There is no mention anywhere in this legislation. All we seem to have is the minister's promise that as a matter of government policy Telesat Canada will continue to provide satellite services to the north.
With all due respect to the minister, whom I respect rightly as an hon. member, Canadians have heard promises from this government before. Such phrases as jobs, jobs, jobs still ring in the ears of Canadians across this country. In particular, it rings in the ears of the almost
1.5	million Canadians that are unemployed across our country.
Canadians have watched over the last seven years as promise after promise of this government has been dropped, botched or broken.
I would not be surprised if Canadians from the north and the remote areas of our country do not feel secure because this government has stated that it promises to ensure that Telesat Canada will continue to provide satellite facilities to their regions.
I would be very surprised if a promise from this government will put to rest the fear that these essential services could be jeopardized by this legislation.
Unless Telesat's role in serving the north is in this legislation, I believe that northerners will have good reason to be concerned that that service could be in jeopardy. Even if the government's promise is fulfilled and satellite services to the north are continued, there is
no mention or there is no promise of which I am aware that would commit the government to ensure that these services are provided at the same level and quality as they are now. That promise could be a very hollow promise if the quality of satellite service to the north is diminished.
A second area of concern that I have about this legislation is the government's decision to privatize Telesat Canada through an open bidding process as opposed to a public share offering. Even Telesat's vice-president of finance and administration, Fred Bartlett, has expressed his preference for a public share offer. He is quoted last May in the Financial Post as saying:
If you want to ensure that Telesat is maintained as a separate entity
and if you want to make sure there's competition within the industry,
public ownership is a good way of going about it.
Those are the words of the vice-president of finance and administration of Telesat.
The open bidding process could provide a great opportunity for a controlling interest in Telesat to fall into the hands of one owner. Of course what this would do, or could do, is reduce the level of competition in an already highly concentrated telecommunication industry.
If that owner happened to be a national carrier, such as Telecom Canada or Unitel, it is conceivable that Telesat could be managed in a way that provides a competitive advantage to the controlling company. In addition, if the controlling company in Telesat was placed with a telephone company there is a possibility that the future direction of Telesat would go in the interests of the telephone industry at the expense of the television cable industry. I suppose that it is only fair to say that the same could be in reverse.
If this scenario is a possibility, then I think the government should take precautions to ensure that it does not take place. In reading the government's own release, it seems that there will be no restriction on who bids for the shares other than the 20 per cent non-resident ownership limit.
I assume that would open the door for the telephone industry to take control of Telesat if it put forward the highest bid. That is a matter that I certainly hope the committee will look at in great detail.
November 19, 1991

Another concern that I want to mention this afternoon is the so-called loosening of restrictions such as Telesat's buy Canada policy that this legislation could very well bring about. Has the government examined the kind of an impact that this could have on Canadian firms which have supplied the goods and services to Telesat?
If Telesat is no longer obligated to purchase from Canadian suppliers, how many Canadian jobs will be jeopardized? I understand certainly that Canada has got to be prepared to compete internationally, and I understand the need to avoid protectionist trade policies. But if this government is planning to allow Telesat to purchase from abroad, is it prepared to assist the Canadian companies and employees who would be jeopardized and damaged as a result of this decision?
There are a lot of concerns about this legislation. I have only mentioned three here this afternoon, and I know others have already been raised. I am sure as the debate continues there will be more concerns brought forward. There are questions to be asked of the government's motives in bringing this forward, questions to be asked of who will be best served by the bill-Canadians, business interests or the government itself? There are questions about the continuation and improvement of services to the north and the remote regions of our country. There are concerns about the decision of the government to sell its shares through the open bidding process rather than a public share offer. There are concerns about how this legislation will affect the Canadian firms that supply Telesat Canada and the jobs of its employees.
I appreciate the opportunity to speak on this matter. I expect that this bill will be thoroughly scrutinized before committee where I hope that some of these concerns will be answered.

Mr. Speaker, what we have here is a fundamental difference in philosophy. This government believes that the government should not be involved in things that can be done probably more economically and more efficiently in the private sector. Whereas the fundamental philosophy of the party of my hon. friend opposite, the hon. member for Chambly who just spoke, is: Why should something be done competitively in the free marketplace if it can be done more expensively and involve more people by the government? With that he speaks at great length about Petro-Canada and its place in the Canadian oil industry.
I would refer him to a better example, one that more truly reflects the philosophy of this government, the example of Air Canada and its predecessor, Trans-Canada Airlines. I remind him that in 1937 it was a Conservative government that introduced and created Trans-Canada Airlines which subsequently became Air Canada.
It was also a Conservative government that instituted and created the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Why? Because there was a public need, a need for government to move in and provide a service that was not being created in the private sector. So they were created.
Let me follow the example of Air Canada. I notice that he did not mention Air Canada in his remarks. The airline developed at a time when there was not an airline and there was one needed. There was a national air service required and it was created. Now, some 50-odd years later, we find that there is all kinds of competition within the airline industry in North America. Indeed there were two trans-national carriers and we had a situation where the people of Canada, the taxpayers of Canada, were subsidizing the maintenance of one of those services while the other service competed in the private sector and had to make it on its own without benefit of government subsidization.

Government Orders
This government quite properly proceeded to privatize Air Canada, bringing significant revenues to the Crown, while at the same time creating fair competition in the marketplace.
I read the words of the chairman of the board of Air Canada who had advocated privatization. He was writing after privatization of how the airline had been, I guess I might say somewhat like myself, too fat and needed to be sheared down so that it would work more effectively. That is precisely what has happened with Air Canada.
Air Canada, one of the finest airlines in the world today, is competing very effectively with Canadian Airlines International without a drain on the taxpayer of Canada.
My hon. friend spoke about the many taxes that have been introduced in the last few years. I want to tell my hon. friend as one member of Parliament who supports the actions of this government that I wish we could get rid of all those taxes. I have not met any of my constituents that like paying taxes. However, the problem is that people want services and in order to provide services we have to raise revenue through taxation. That is what was done with the various taxes.
If the government had not inherited a $38 billion deficit and a $16 billion operating deficit, we would not have had to increase taxes in order to pay for the sins and the debts of those who were here before us.
With respect to Telesat I just very briefly will make this last point so my hon. friend can respond. I would remind him that there was a need for public intervention to see that Telesat was established in the way that it was to develop and provide satellite based commercial telecommunications services in Canada. This objective has now been achieved.
The government is no longer providing capital or operating funds for Telesat and no longer has any reason to continue its investment in Telesat. Therefore we say it is time to pass it on to the private sector in which it can continue to grow, develop and serve Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I think the purpose of Crown corporations in this country since the beginning of time has been to use these vehicles as serving a public policy function. I think in the last few years, especially with the government's
Government Orders
approach, we have been too easily tempted when times are tough or if a company all of a sudden showed a little bit of a financial burden to dump it too quickly. As a result we have a policy that has been instituted and implemented by this government which basically led to the dismantling of this country's finest business assets.
I am really having problems with this because as I go through the list I do not see the real benefit to Canadians by the actions that it has taken. For example, let us start off with Air Canada because it has been raised here. The first share offering of Air Canada, which is a company that the government privatized, I guess it was three years ago, was sold at about $1.50 before market share, and this was assessed by some of the best analysts in the country. The proceeds from the first offering did not go into the national treasury. They went back into the corporation which effectively inflated the remaining shares.
Look at CN hotels. I am not convinced that the land acquisition was really taken into account properly. Concerning CN En Route, we know from the many times in this House that the land was worth almost twice as much as the government received. In other words, the Government of Canada had $29 million in proceeds from the CN En Route project, but the person who bought it for the $29 million turned around and sold the land alone for close to $46 million. On it goes. Just think of all the things that this government has privatized such as Canadair, the company which makes our Challenger jet and our water bombers, Canadian Arsenals and de Havilland. It is an incredible list.
Let us look at de Havilland. Here was an instrument of public policy in which the taxpayers of Canada spent close to a billion dollars in research and development. We made some of the finest aircraft in the world, the Dash-7 and the Dash-8, and we were starting to get a full book for these planes. Now all of sudden because the Boeing company is running into trouble and is trying to stabilize its own act at home the first on the chopping block is the Canadian subsidiary.
Had de Havilland remained a Crown corporation then today we could have maintained this as an instrument of public policy and the 4,000 direct jobs in Ontario would not be in jeopardy as they are today. I give full marks to the Prime Minister and the Premier of Ontario who are in Paris today scrambling trying to save de Havilland, but

Government Orders
not for the Canadian taxpayer; they are almost begging an offshore buyer to come and pick up the pieces.
Here is an example in which the government, in its haste to dismantle a major piece of industry from a sector of our economy which was so vital in terms of global trading, basically acted rashly and quickly. The only people who really benefited in this particular case were the brokers. The national treasury certainly did not.
Take a look at the Northern Canada Power Commission. The government sold it to the Northwest Territories. We subsidize through transfers from the national government the Northwest Territories year in and year out. This is nothing more than a gymnastic of figures. Who is the government kidding on this? On we go with Teleglobe, CNCP Telecommunications, the Canada Development Corporation, Fishery Products International and Varity. We saw what happened with Varity. Once the final private placement was done on Varity off it went to Buffalo.
I have nothing against the decisions that businesses are taking. Once these businesses are in private hands it is the responsibility of the boards of directors of these companies which report to their shareholders to be concerned about the bottom line, about profit. The business of business is profit, but the business of government is people. That has been, should be and should continue to be, the filter that we use when we are going through the analysis of whether we should sell off or dismantle these Crown corporations.
In the case of the bill before us, Bill C-38 respecting Telesat Canada, we use a very simple example. We are talking about communications in the north. There is no direct provision in this legislation for maintaining services forever in the north. How could there be? We cannot sell a Crown corporation to a private person and then dictate what the business plan is going to be for the next 10 years. The objectives are totally different.
We may say we are going to make sure it does this for two or three years, but invariably it happens that time after time all of a sudden the particular corporation loses money. It will come back to Ottawa and get all its high powered lobbyists in place to come around and lobby us and say: "Listen, we are losing money on this company.
You must get behind us. You must support the grant or the tax-free loan or get cabinet behind us if you want us to maintain our system in the north".
What do we do? We get behind them. We get behind them. In essence we have given away the control of this public policy instrument but we continue to fund it. What is the point? We are better to realize that these Crown corporations are public policy instruments. They are used to create jobs, to maintain jobs and to provide a national standard of services in some of the key sectors of this economy so that a person in Prince Edward Island can get the same kind of service that a person can get in downtown Toronto or a person in the Northwest Territories can get the same kind of service as we in downtown Toronto have. As soon as we move away the Crown corporation, the public policy instrument, and give it to a private sector outfit which has a different objective, we essentially break down the ability to deliver a national standard whether it is communication or service or whatever. The whole problem with this government is that it does not think in terms of national standards. It does not realize that by creating these national standards and services you get a national will. It is from that national will that we continue to fight against all the forces that are trying to move in and push this country around. When you break down region by region the way this government tends to do, it is very tough to keep us together. It is very tough to fight the economic forces that tend to move in on us.
I will give you the example of the de Havilland corporation in my city. Its skilled labour force in Toronto is responsible for the Dash-8 which is probably one of the finest aircraft in the world in terms of short take off and landing. Can you imagine that as we stand in this House we have to be worried that it may not continue as an entity? We go out there cup in hand and ask Italy and France to get a joint venture deal together and please buy out de Havilland.
The whole thing is absolutely crazy. The Canadian taxpayer invested a billion dollars in the research and development to put de Havilland on the international map. Then after all of the taxpayers' start-up costs and its key expenses have been put into the thing, a full book,
November 19, 1991

all of a sudden we turn the control over to an organization run out of the United States.
When times are tough in the United States what happens? They are not going to shut down an operation in the United States. I mean how naive can we get. They look out around the world and say: "Where can we cut costs because we are no different from anyone else? We want earnings per share". They look up to Canada and say: "Let's shut down de Elavilland. Let's give away de Havilland because there is absolutely no way that it is going to help our earnings per share in the United States".
I think that this government's privatization program has been a disaster. I am not against business doing a job on its own. A government should only be operating a business if the private sector says to us that it is not profitable. If it is not profitable but we need to maintain a national service or a product that we think may need start-up costs and in the long term we can hand it over, terrific. But we are taking some of these Crown corporations that are jewels and have made the Canadian taxpayer proud. I am proud of Petro-Canada. I am proud that I was a part of the government that put the Petro-Canada package together.
There may have been some flaws in putting the deal together and maybe some of the commissions were a little excessive. But it gave us a window into the oil industry which previously had been ripping off the Canadian taxpayer to the tune of hundreds and hundreds of millions of dollars a year. Petro-Canada was a galvanizing agent in this country. It pulled us together as politicians. I know even this government, from a political perspective, has given subtle direction to Petro-Canada in terms of using it for public policy. What is wrong with the national government having a window in the oil business? There is no country in the world that does not have a strong window in the oil business. As I said earlier, we might have made some mistakes in putting the deal together, but that is no reason to try and dismantle it.
These members want to dismantle everything. This government wants to retreat from governing.
We wonder why they came to Ottawa. They are supposed to come to Ottawa to govern the country not to retreat from governing the country. If they do not want
Government Orders
to sell it to the private sector they want to give it to the provinces.
It is like FIRA. I see the member from Calgary and I will never forget the very first night I met him. We got into a tremendous debate over the Foreign Investment Review Agency. We wanted to have checks on foreign investment coming in here. We did not just want their money. We wanted them to put money into research and development. We wanted them to do some manufacturing here.
Now-what do we have? We have a situation where they can waltz into this country now and just about do whatever they want. But if times get rough there is no regulation for continuing to do business here. They just leave. That is why we have this flight of manufacturing organizations and capital, the likes of which this country has never seen before.
We had strong Crown corporations in these various sectors to try to maintain a window in these industries and use them to try to negotiate jobs. There may have been times when we sold some of those products at prices that may have been on the low side, but as long as we had people working rather than sitting at home we felt it was a good instrument of public policy.
This government must realize now that its business plan for this country is not working. It is not working in spite of the liquidation, the giveaway, the sell-off and the paper shuffle of Crown corporations. It has sold off more Crown corporations in a three or four year period than probably in the history of this cBountry.
In spite of all that, they have still doubled the debt and the deficit. They do not have a handle on the unemployment situation and they have boxed themselves in. They cannot even get any job creation programs going because they are boxed in. They cannot raise taxes because they have raised them 40 times. They cannot go to the financial markets because they are burning up their credibility there.
Why can they not review their attitude on these Crown corporations and realize that it is a phoney game to say that they are going to reduce the deficit by selling off these Crown corporations when they know in fact that is not really what is happening. It is a gymnastics of figures and it does not do a darned thing to help the balance sheet of this country. It does not do a darned thing to put

people back together. It does not do anything on a long-term basis.
Can we imagine the Prime Minister of Canada today having to almost beg to get a buyer for a Crown corporation like de Havilland? I mean it is sick. There is no way. It is one of the finest corporations in Canada, but we lost our leverage. We lost our control by selling it off to Boeing.

We did not lose any money when we put the job creation factor and the R and D factor into the pot. They talk about international competitiveness. They do not even have control of the aircraft sector when they give it away to the Americans.
If you have a marketing and sales guy to sell Dash-8s, where does he get his direction right now? He gets it from Boeing in the United States. When you control it you can put those marketing guys on the road at the Paris Air Show or wherever you go and you can fill the book. You can decide what the prices are and you can keep everybody working.
I think it is a heck of a lot better to train people and maintain skilled craftsmen than to have people on the unemployment lines. Think of the indirect jobs that you control through all of these Crown corporations.
I am not saying that I condone waste. I do not. I am not saying we could not have made these corporations more efficient. We could have. You are doing the same thing with the airport.
Look at what you did with Terminal 3 in Toronto. If the public of Canada ever knew what was going on in Terminal 3 right now there would be a revolt in this country. It is a non-optional use facility right now. You know the person who bought it cannot meet its financial regulations and you guys are in a box. You are damned if you do and damned if you do not, trying to fix the problem. That is what is wrong.
You do not see these as instruments of public policy making where you can keep people employed. I would rather have a higher deficit and have everybody working than have the deficit you have now with 2.5 million people unemployed. You have the country in a state of chronic depression and you do not know where you are going. That is the problem. You do not have a single idea over there and you have given the shop away. You have practically destroyed the country.

speechtext: It being five o'clock p.m., pursuant to Standing Order 30(6), the House will now proceed to the consideration of Private Members' Business as listed on today's Order Paper.

The House resumed from Tuesday, October 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. Arseneault that Bill C-211, an act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act (temporary community service), be read the second time and referred to Legislative Committee A.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to speak on Bill C-211.
The purpose of the bill, to refresh the memory of the House, is to amend section 14 of the Unemployment Insurance Act to ensure that persons in temporary service to the community as jurors or emergency workers, in other words in a community service, are not regarded as disqualified from a benefit merely because of their participation in such an activity.
I have a number of points that I want to make in a preliminary sense, realizing that I have another nine and a half minutes to speak here. You may wonder why I am speaking on this, Mr. Speaker. There are three reasons. The first reason is that I was very impressed with the way that the member for Restigouche-Chaleur put forward this motion because I think it is a wrong that needs to be righted. It is a wrong that can be righted by the agreement of all in the House, and I will be very disappointed if I find that there is an intention to talk this bill out so that it does not really come to the point where it can in fact be effective.
The second reason is that I am familiar with the Restigouche-Chaleur area. I have spent many a day up there, going back really I suppose too long to remember. I have a great affection for the people in that area. They
November 19, 1991

are not unlike the constituents whom I represent in Bonavista-Trinity-Conception. It is not a rich part of the world. It is an area where, if there are any injustices to be righted, I think we should take all the time and effort that we can in this House to look after the little guy and the little woman. That is what it is all about and this is what we are trying to do on this side of the House. I hope that members on the other side of the House and on this side that are not in my party will pay attention to this fairly basic point in principle.
The third reason I want to speak on this is that it concerns the Unemployment Insurance Act. I have spoken many times in this House on this subject and the things that have bothered me, the people in my riding in Atlantic Canada, and I suppose for that matter all over Canada, going back to Bill C-21 and that kind of thing.
I am not going to rehash the ills of that bill but will get into the substantive debate on this issue. The government will have to recognize that there is an inequity in this particular section of the Unemployment Insurance Act. I do not think much of an effort is going to be required to change this bill.
In so doing, it will indicate some flexibility on the government side in a positive sense so that it can take the bill and make the amendments.
When any member of the community, male or female, who is drawing unemployment insurance represents their community by participating in jury duty or any other emergency community duty can be forgiven and still be considered to be employable under the Unemployment Insurance Act. In fact, when they are performing this duty, they can indeed still qualify for unemployment insurance.
What we are dealing with here is the possibility of the government showing some flexibility with respect to the Unemployment Insurance Act. God knows, it has shown a lot of flexibility in the Unemployment Insurance Act. In the relatively short time that I have been in this House, I have seen more changes made to this particular act and more changes made to what I believe was the intent of the act when it was put forward in 1940 as a safety net for Canadians who were out of work. It has made many changes and has indicated a degree of flexibility that unfortunately has always been in the negative sense.

Let me just give some poor examples. I am going to remind the government that these are poor examples. When it sits down in the sober light of dawn to look at and see a chance to continue and to discharge its flexibility in a positive sense, those people likely to be cut off will qualify under this safety net and will be given some consideration.
When I first came to this House almost four years ago to the day, indeed before I became a member of Parliament, I recall the hon. minister from Newfoundland, who was representing the government at the time, now the hon. Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, in St. John's, Newfoundland, responded to some questions with respect to free trade. I know he does not like to be reminded of this, but I do have to remind him because the content and the substance of what he said was: "You are out there worried about unemployment insurance and the safety net and the level playing field and all these fear mongers like Mifflin and all his other people that are out saying you are going to be cut back on unemployment insurance, do not pay any attention to them because I can assure you, I have it from the Prime Minister, that there will be absolutely no changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act".
That was in October. I learn now that when we sat in this House after the election of November 21, I was horrified to find that on November 22, less than a month after the minister had made that statement, the changes that ended up in Bill C-21. They were so controversial that I presented 40,000 signatures of my constituents in this House against that bill. It was in April that the hon. minister of the day, sitting over there, produced the changes that horrified this side of the House. In effect it did a number of things. What it did essentially is take the government out of unemployment insurance. It took away in my riding and particularly Atlantic Canada which was hurting very much, the job development programs on which people unfortunately and regrettably had to rely. These are gone now. We just had section 25, which really does not give employability, but just considers those who have stamps. It raises the level of those stamps. The job creation programs as I knew them and as I nurtured and encouraged them have disappeared. This has been very hurtful to my riding.
The other point that showed flexibility is that the formula for unemployment insurance is that the employer paid 43 per cent. It was 1.4 times more than the

November 19, 1991
Private Members' Business
employee, who paid 31 per cent. In those days, the government paid 26 per cent. Now the government pays nothing. It started off at $1.95 per $100 of insurable earnings for the employee. It is now going to go up to $3 which is a 60 per cent increase in three years. The employer paid $2.73 per $100 insurable earnings. It has now gone up and will go up on January 1 to $4.20, 60 per cent. That is flexibility? We can show flexibility in taking away programs from people. We can show flexibility in taking the government out of the UIC business. We can show flexibility in taking away job creation programs for people who do not have jobs, particularly in areas where the fishing industry this year and the year before is just terrible. If flexibility can be shown in the negative sense, then why can the government not now show some flexibility in the positive sense.
I read all the correspondence that came from Marsha Valdron to the hon. member for Restigouche-Chaleur. She was incredulous that because she performed a duty and because she was honest in what she did, she was being penalized by the system. I read all the correspondence and I read the letters that went back and forth and the system is saying to her: "Yes, but that is what the act says and besides, jury duty is a provincial responsibility".
Here is the one case where the little person has taken up the cudgel. She is saying to us in this House: "I am one of many who have been treated this way and I would like to have some redress. I would like people to consider this". Well, we are considering this and I am sure there will be a government member speaking very soon.
I know there are many government members who want to vote for this. I will be very hurt if I find that the partisan system has designated x number of people to vote against this, because it is no skin off the government's back to vote this. It is not going to hurt anybody to show the flexibility in a positive sense, to make allowances for those people who discharge their civic duties. I think this is one chance.
I just heard what the hon. member for Broadview- Greenwood had to say with respect to ideas and creativity. I agree with him generally, of course. This is one chance for this government to show that it has creativity and concern for the average person, what is referred to as the common man, the common person, the common woman in this case.
If the government could pause and show some consideration in this area and show some compassion and feeling for ordinary Canadians, I do not think it would do it any harm. It would do it the world of good and do the country some good at this particular point in our history.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to participate in this debate on Bill C-211. There are fundamental flaws in this amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act. This bill seems laudable in theory, but in practice it promises chaos.
This bill threatens to open up a Pandora's box of parallel amendments that would burden the UI system with complex administrative spinoffs and open-ended cost increases.
The response must clearly be to reject this well-intentioned but ill-conceived legislation. In support of rejection, my colleagues in this House will be presenting sound jurisdictional and financial arguments. In rejecting this bill, we would like to make it clear, if any doubt still remains, that we have no argument with the general objective implicit in the proposed amendment.
A more relevant, less financially punitive system of compensation for Canadians that fulfil temporary civic responsibilities and community services such as jury duty and fire fighting, is a concept few of us here today could disagree with. That point was made repeatedly on October 8 when C-211 first came before the House. There can be little question that compensation must be raised to more realistic levels to ensure that community and civic services retain their essential place in Canadian society.
However, applying this compensation to the UI program remains not only inappropriate fiscally and jurisdictionally, it also plants the seeds for a scenario of inexorable add-ons to a social safety net already straining at the seams. The current bill for our UI program is $20 billion. If we open up the compensatory door suggested by C-211, an over-burdened program could find itself subject to a blizzard of so-called special cases that would end where, we do not know.
November 19, 1991

Leaving aside for the moment the administrative implications of this scenario, the fact is that adequate compensation for civic duties is not in any case the responsibility of the unemployment insurance program. Yes, there is a real problem in the low rates of compensation paid through provincial justice systems, but the solution to this problem surely does not rest with the unemployment insurance program. Yes, the compensation paid by the provinces to Canadians serving on juries is generally far less than UI benefits but the question the House should be asking is: Since when were UI benefits designed to subsidize provincial judicial systems?
In each part of the country it is incumbent on the provincial or territorial authorities to look closely at jury duty compensation schemes and adjust them to more accurately reflect the needs of those fulfilling part-time civic and community duties. Quite obviously it is not through the resources of the unemployment insurance system that we should be addressing the question of compensation for fulfilling a civic duty.
It is within the judicial system of each province that the resolution for this problem lies. This is the appropriate course jurisdictionally. Of that there can be little question.
It is also appropriate from a practical point of view because it is simply much easier to resolve this problem through relatively straightforward administrative changes at the provincial or territorial level than to try to deal with it through the UI system.
Amendments are intended to refine, clarify or somehow improve existing legislation. This amendment if adopted would not improve in any way existing UI legislation. Rather, it would severely complicate it which should not be the effect of legislative amendments presented before this House.
This amendment through its emphasis on the creation of an increasing number of exceptions does nothing to help the UI system to better serve Canadians. It simply asks the system to do things for which it was not created and is not responsible.
The question before the House is: Do we embark on rewriting the Unemployment Insurance Act or do we suggest in the strongest terms to the provinces and the
Private Members' Business
territories that they compensate people fulfilling their civic duty at rates consistent with 1991 wage levels? This question of adequate compensation is an important one and the hon. member should be commended for bringing it to the attention of the House. However, Canada's unemployment insurance system is clearly the wrong tool with which to tackle the problem.
I urge the members of this House to ask themselves again: What does this legislation mean? I urge them to ask: Where would it end? I urge them finally to let our unemployment insurance system do its job and let the provinces do theirs.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity on behalf of my colleagues in the New Democratic Party to address and support Bill C-211, an act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act. For the record, I would simply like to read in the additional words to be added to section 14 of the Unemployment Insurance Act by the bill before us.
It says under section 14: "A claimant is not entitled to be paid benefit for any working day in a benefit period for which the claimant fails to prove that the claimant was either (a) capable of and available for work and unable to obtain suitable employment on that day (b) incapable of work by reason of prescribed illness, injury or quarantine on that day and that he would be otherwise available for work". It would add to that the provision "(c) engaged in jury service or (d) serving temporarily as a result of an emergency as a fire fighter, flood control worker, rescue worker, provider of food or shelter or other such worker for the community".
My colleague across the way just said that the UI act and the unemployment insurance system was the wrong tool and suggested that when the unemployment insurance system was first devised, it was not created for such a purpose as illustrated by the bill before us and it was not responsible for looking after such things as jury service, emergency services or compensating people for engaging in such necessary public interest actions.
Over the years, while it may not be the best social cost accounting we have added, under several different governments of at least two different stripes, a number of

November 19, 1991
Private Members' Business
objectives and a number of reasons for receiving UI benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act. These objectives also have nothing to do with the original reason for putting unemployment insurance into place. For us to now say that it is the wrong tool I think is attempting to rewrite an awful lot of history. We and all parties have found it very convenient to use this system to compensate people for a number of reasons that have nothing to do with the vagaries of the marketplace and whether or not an employee or a group of employees find themselves out of work through no fault of their own.
For instance, we have added sickness leave to the unemployment insurance system. What that has to do with the vagaries of the industrial marketplace I do not know.
We have added maternity leave to the UI system. What that has to do with the vagaries of the marketplace I do not know.
We have added job training and what that has to do with someone being out of work through the vagaries of the marketplace I do not know.
There is the matter of relocation of employees from one section of the country to another. We have subsidized the wages of employees through job training. We have subsidized, over the years, the wages of employees in job sharing scenarios.
These are all in terms of social cost accounting the kind of activities which would more properly have been borne by the general revenue of the nation and not by a system which raised its moneys largely in the past through the contributions of the employees and employers with no regard to ability to pay.
Now we have had the government retreat from any public subsidy of this system. We have collectively agreed that all of these various obligations regarding sickness insurance, maternity insurance, job training payments, subsidy of wages for job sharing and the subsidy of job training, which it could be argued should be part of the education system, by vote of this House on a number of occasions that these will all be paid by contributions of employees and employers.
Having agreed to all of that because we have found this a very convenient system in which to attach these various schemes which we had deemed to be in the public interest, what causes us now to say: "Oh, this is an inappropriate mechanism". If we are going to argue that let us be consistent and put all of these other matters back in the regime which provides for their financing out of general revenue and not simply payments from employees and employers without any regard to then-ability to pay. Those are societal responsibilities.
If we are not going to return all of these to being financed out of general revenue, what is wrong with adding what is going to be a relatively minor cost to an area which obviously is one of some shared responsibility?
The minister in his letter to members of Parliament on October 8, 1991 suggested that the subject of juries and juiy duty falls under provincial jurisdiction. Well that may well be so, but the Criminal Code and the criminal law and the administration of justice is certainly a matter that falls very much both within provincial jurisdiction and federal jurisdiction. It is, therefore, quite appropriate we feel that a measure to provide those who are fulfilling a mandated public responsibility by serving on juries or serving in various emergency services required by their communities, and certainly endorsed by both the federal and provincial authorities, should not be penalized for fulfilling their public obligations.
While the provinces certainly have not borne what most of us would regard as being an appropriate share of any burden to see that Canadians that take part in these activities are not penalized for doing so, and certainly the rates which they provide under the various provincial jurisdictions should be increased, that does not let the federal government off the hook for contributing what should be its share of seeing to it that persons who do fulfil their public duty in the ways pointed out by this Bill C-211 should not be penalized for so doing.
We agree with the goals. We in the New Democratic Party also believe in a UI system which has been conveniently used, and many would argue properly used, to assist Canadians on a wide variety of endeavours which we in this House and people across the country have deemed to be appropriate and in the public interest. We also agree that the matter of serving on juries and the question of providing emergency services are also areas for which Canadians have a right to expect that they shall not be penalized by actions of this government, either by omission or commission.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to take part in this debate on the bill introduced by the hon. member, a bill whose intent will, I am sure, be applauded by all members of this House.
However, we must be able to rely on citizens who act responsibly, who are called for jury duty or who give up some of their time to help members of their communities.
This country has over five million volunteers, and I think I am not overstating my case when I say that these people represent the very essence of civic duty in this country. I am sure all members will agree that the volunteer concept contributes immensely to the quality of life of Canadians.
The issue is not whether citizens on jury duty or working on a volunteer basis as firefighters or rescue workers, for instance, should be compensated through the unemployment insurance plan. Of course they should. The question is whether the hon. member's bill is the right way to deal with this problem.
We are all familiar with the role that insurance plays in our lives. Almost all Canadians have some kind of insurance policy: life insurance, home or accident insurance, automobile insurance and unemployment insurance. We pay our premiums and we receive payments when necessary.
However, Mr. Speaker-and I am convinced this is an important point-we can only receive payments if we observe the terms of our insurance contract. The insurance company may sympathize with our situation, but if we do not meet the terms of our insurance policy, we cannot receive compensation. Private sector insurance could not survive if it made an exception every time a customer argues that he is entitled to compensation although he is not eligible under the terms of the insurance contract.
Since the Canadian government is financially responsible for its programs, they must be administered in the same way. There are criteria for every government expenditure. The federal government would be accused, and rightly so, of being financially irresponsible if it did not require claimants to at least observe the eligibility criteria.
Private Members' Business
The hon. member argued that his bill would change the criteria and allow unemployment insurance recipients who are on jury duty or who work as volunteers on an emergency team to receive benefits. However, I may remind the hon. member that although other members and I fully support the purpose of this bill, we do not think the amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act is in order.
The Unemployment Insurance Act is supposed to help workers that are temporarily unemployed and are seeking employment. Canadians do not pay unemployment insurance premiums to compensate jury members or volunteers that work here and there, praiseworthy though their work may be.
What, in fact, would be the impact of Bill C-211? Let's think about it. Would the repercussions of this amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act be as simple as they look? What could be the consequences for the government if this bill were passed?
Let us look more closely at the bill put forward by our colleague. Under paragraph (c), UI benefits would be paid to persons who could be, and I quote:
-engaged in jury service.
Now, Mr Speaker, for how long? The way the government looks at this matter is not unreasonable. We already give two days of grace, which is a reasonable period, before questioning the claimant's availability.
The hon. member's bill does not provide for any time limit for the period where the UI claimant could serve for jury duty while drawing benefits.
A policy without strictly defined limits would simply not be practical and definitely would be irresponsible. Some trials drag on for months. The provincial judicial systems are responsible for jury service. The benefits paid by the federal government under its unemployment insurance plan were never intended to compensate citizens called up for jury duty for indeterminate periods because provincial governments would not pay them sufficiently.
Let's take paragraph (d) of Bill C-211. Under this paragraph, unemployment insurance benefits would be paid to a claimant, and I quote:
