-serving temporarily as a result of an emergency as a firefighter, flood control worker, rescue worker, provider of food or shelter or other such worker for the community.
What do we mean by temporarily? A fire in a house might last just a few hours, but the time required to control a forest fire depends on the weather conditions as well as several other factors.
My colleage will surely agree that the unemployment insurance plan could be faced with a considerable increase in costs if the word temporarily meant indefinitely-
Under paragraph (d), benefits would also be paid to a claimant "serving as a provider of food or shelter or other such worker for the community". What does my colleague mean by other such worker? What are the limitations of that volunteer work?
The bill gives great discretion as regards the interpretation of that clause. There is no question that the intention of my hon. colleague is praiseworthy, but to pass this bill might be like opening a pandora's box and create a real administrative and financial nightmare. And how many people would benefit from these provisions in the bill? Probably not a large number, not enough to justify the additional administrative costs that would result from the implementation of these new provisions.
As I said, we are all grateful to the citizens that show public spiritedness. These people show a dedication that is largely responsible for the strength of our great nation. However, the Unemployment Insurance Act is not the channel that must be used to insure, to reward or to protect the salary of jurors or volunteers, regardless of their contribution to our society. If we eliminate the requirement to actively look for a job, we run the risk of transforming unemployment insurance benefits into a form of welfare assistance, and that is not the reason why Canadians contribute to the unemployment insurance program.
The bill introduced by the hon. member is well-intentioned, but it has nothing to do with the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act. After all, people on a jury do have a job, even if it carries extremely low compensation. It would run counter to the principle of the act to pay benefits to a person with a job. The problem the hon. member is trying to deal with should be raised with provinces because they are the ones who give
a meagre compensation to jurors in their judicial systems. The hon. member should look at it this way: since the responsibility lies with the provinces, he should submit his very worth while proposal to them.
So I am sure that if our colleague withdrew his bill, he could easily obtain a lot of support to explain the situation to provincial governments and to ask them to examine their policy with regards to the remuneration of jurors and of volunteers involved in community service.
I am certain, Mr. Speaker, that our colleague will get considerable support on this issue. But it is essential to bring the issue to the attention of those who have jurisdiction in that area and can study the matter. That means that this issue has to be submitted to the provincial legislatures, not to this government.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to publicly congratulate my colleague from Restigouche-Chaleur for an initiative I found very laudable. Why? Because it tries to correct an injustice.
I have heard all the hon. members who have addressed the issue so far and have supported it. They wholeheartedly agree with what he is trying to achieve, that is to correct an unfair situation occurring at this very moment. But as they often do, they even blame the bureaucrats sometimes for doing so, they say it is not clear enough, it needs to be better defined, if we do this, we might create some other problems. I say let us go ahead, let us do something. We are faced with an injustice, something that should not happen.
And here my colleague has suggested a solution. I congratulate him for doing so. Let me tell you something else.

It is not just myself or my colleague and others who have said there is a problem here which needs correction. I would like to quote from a document. It is a newspaper article which calls the UI rule stupid.
Who would say such a thing? A judge who excuses potential jurors because he really felt that this particular rule, one which denied benefits to people who served as jurors or emergency workers, was incorrect. He felt even more strongly than I did on that particular day because he called it a stupid rule.
November 19, 1991

Private Members' Business
What happens? You receive unemployment insurance if you are without employment, if you paid sufficient benefits. A person may be called away for jury duty or some other emergency work such as fire fighting or what have you. If that were to last more than two days one would lose the benefits. One would lose the benefits, but one would also be unable to look for work and obviously, if you are fighting fires or serving on jury duty, it is very difficult to be looking for work.
It is an injustice. It is not correct. It is inappropriate and something must be done.
Let us review together, just so that we do not lose sight of what my colleague from Restigouche-Chaleur was attempting, the purpose of the Unemployment Insurance Act. The purpose of the UI act was "to promote the economic and social security of Canadians by supporting workers that lose their jobs".
If you have lost your job and you are getting this kind of benefit and you do your community work, your civic duty, clearly you ought not to be penalized. Some of my colleagues have indicated that there are other ways of compensating. I suspect, although I cannot speak for my colleague, that what he wants is the situation corrected. This is one way of correcting it. If others, particularly government members, want to bring forward bills that will correct it, we would be delighted to look at them. However we do not want just talk. We do not want just evasion. We do not want people side-stepping the issue. We want people dealing with it head on.
People who are unemployed or who are called away to do civic duty about which they have no choice basically but to say yes, and they probably want to, should not be penalized because they do what the community, the province or their country requires them to do.
Let me remind members as well of another very important fundamental principle of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Equity has always been an important part of unemployment insurance. Many amendments were made to eliminate the inequities contained in the original legislation. Interesting. There was a reduction in waiting periods during the 1950's, more categories of jobs became insurable. Additional contingencies of sickness, maternity and retirement were covered. Entrance requirements were lowered and benefit rates became more generous.
I point that out because clearly what my colleague is seeking is not unusual. It is not off the wall. These amendments were brought forward to correct injustices, inequities to make the system more just, and that is what my colleague from Restigouche-Chaleur is attempting to do.
I want to remind people as well that the Unemployment Insurance Act is intended to provide income security to citizens, not penalize them when they are under obligation to exercise their civic duties. That is the crux of the matter. That is the very heart of it.
All members of Parliament have constituents that may be faced with having to carry out their civic responsibilities either as jurors or emergency workers. Therefore, members from all parties it seems to me should support a bill which intends to address an injustice, a glaring inequity.
I just cannot believe we could not come to some agreement here. Either we support this particular bill, or we come forward immediately with another avenue that will in fact do the same thing. Let us not penalize people who do their civic duty.
I want to remind colleagues as well, and I want to quote my colleague's press release: "This amendment that has been brought forward will ensure that persons in temporary service to the community, such as jurors or emergency workers are not regarded as disqualified from unemployment insurance benefits because of their participation in such an activity".
That is the crux, that is the issue, that is the centrepiece. That is what we want to do.

I think we have here an incredible opportunity to address a very minor issue, that is so important for many people, and to correct an injustice. Why should we not go ahead? Why not agree for once on an issue like this one, on something that will allow us to correct an injustice? We all agree that people who give some of their time to their communities, their province, and their country, should not be penalized? Why not correct this situation?

November 19, 1991
Private Members' Business

This bill, it seems to me, is so commonsensical that we should not even be taking the time to debate it. I do not say that to denigrate the bill because it does address a very important question.
This makes so much sense that there ought to be a mechanism when a colleague comes up with such an idea. It ought to go through that mechanism and be dealt with like that, quickly, immediately: correct it.
If all parties cannot agree here on this one issue, this issue that deals with men and women across the nation, this small issue in relationship to those other issues that we have to deal with but an important one to those people who it touches, how could we possibly dream of coming to some agreement on the big question?

Whether it be major constitutional issues, the economy, social programs, the environment or other key matters which affect every Canadian, if we do not manage to agree on a simple question of this importance, I believe that it will be very difficult indeed to find solutions to the other major issues.

I am here and I notice I have just a bit of time left. I would not only propose that we go forward with my colleague's bill, my colleague from Restigouche-Cha-leur, but I would suggest that we take an opportunity to study the whole of the UI bill after we pass this one.
What he is doing is laudable. It needs to be done. We all know that there are a number of problems with the Unemployment Insurance Act: part-time workers, the variations that exist, the number of hours that you have to work and whether or not you will qualify or not qualify, the ability to upgrade when you are collecting unemployment insurance so that you can in fact hope and dream of a better position later on, the adequacy of the amount that you receive, the whole notion.
My colleague has reminded me of adoptive parents and the contradictions that exist there. I would suggest that we take this particular example, pass it and begin the process of reconstruction.

Let us try to deal with this issue so we can move to other major concerns. Let us set our house in order. Let us make sure that Canadian men and women who need help will get it in an efficient, adequate and timely fashion.

I ask my colleagues to do everything they can to make sure that this bill that my colleague from Restigouche- Chaleur has brought forward will correct an injustice in the Unemployment Insurance Act.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to speak today on this well-intentioned bill. I congratulate the member for Restigouche- Chaleur. It is bills like these that entitle a member of this House to truly deserve the title "honourable".
I do not think anyone here would disagree when I say that the intention behind this bill is an honourable one.
We do not vote on bills solely on the basis of their intent. To do so would be an abdication of our responsibilities. Rather, we scrutinize proposed legislation and having done that, I must say that I believe this bill should not be supported by this House. The reason I say this is primarily a technical one.
First, Mr. Speaker, I invite you to consider the impact of this bill on a program that is funded by two large and important sectors, Canadian employers and Canadian workers. With that in mind, I would like to address the financial implications of this motion on the unemployment insurance program. In doing so, I hope to convince my colleagues that this motion is not viable in today's economic climate, nor is it appropriate in that it crosses into and usurps provincial jurisdiction.
How much would it cost to implement this motion? That is not the essential question. For example, we are unable to estimate the cost of paying UI benefits to volunteer workers, although we do know that it would cost some $2.2 million to extend benefits only to those UI claimants who sat on jury duty in the last fiscal year.
By government standards, $2.2 million may not seem like a large amount of money, and it is not, especially in a $20 billion program like unemployment insurance. But that is not the important issue. The essential question is: What is the purpose of the UIC program and the

jurisdictional responsibility for it, for jury service and for community services?
If we are to judge the motion based solely on the dollar amount for jury duty, I am sure that many members would vote in favour of it. I must warn members, however, that when you look exclusively at cold, hard figures you run the risk of not seeing the broader picture. Therefore, it is critical that we examine other factors which must be taken into account.
Mr. Speaker, you just heard my colleague discuss some of the ramifications of this motion. His remarks clearly indicated that its passage would have numerous spin-off effects. In other words, if this motion passed then future sittings of the House would undoubtedly end up discussing similar such requests and the question of extending UI benefits under other circumstances would be raised again and again.
If we are going to talk about government support for charities or even churches, I would say parenthetically that I would support doing away with the present system of tax credits for charitable donations and donations for churches in favour of a matching dollar program for real charitable work, where community service is being delivered with no more than 20 per cent overhead, instead of making contributions to religious activities. But that is another issue for another day.
Returning to the issue at hand, if requests started to multiply, what would then be the cost? Obviously, neither I nor members on the other side can answer that question. I can guarantee that it will be much higher than the figure I mentioned a moment ago. I hope this will give food for thought to those hon. members who are unequivocal in their support of this motion.
At the very least, I would ask them to contemplate the consequences on those who must contribute a portion of their weekly earnings in supporting this insurance program. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the UI program is financed through premium contributions made by the nation's employers and workers. The federal government provides interim financing, some $1.3 billion in 1992, but ultimately it is the workers and employees who finance the program. I am sure that members would
Private Members' Business
agree with me that Canadians who pay those premiums would be quite apprehensive if any additional burden were placed on the UI program, especially when the cost of that burden cannot be actively calculated.
This is particularly true in light of the announcement made yesterday by the Minister of Employment and Immigration. As you know, he stated that the unemployment insurance premiums of both workers and employers will rise in 1992 by some 7.1 per cent, I believe it was.
I know how reluctant the minister was to make that announcement, but he had no choice. The UI fund is currently operating at a deficit and even the announced premium increases will not reduce that shortfall, they will only maintain the deficit at a manageable level.
Given this reality, I feel it would hardly be prudent to place additional pressures on the UI fund. We simply cannot afford it. It becomes even harder to justify increasing UI premiums when you consider that the money would be spent in areas that clearly fall under provincial jurisdiction.
The comments about fire fighting had me particularly confused because when I was a young geologist I used to work in northern communities quite frequently. Very often unemployment insurance credits were earned during fire fighting. If we made unemployment payable for people who were on fire fighting duty we could readily see that the provincial governments would suddenly refuse to pay people and just conscript them into that service.
Compensation for jurors and emergency volunteer workers is a provincial responsibility. Under these circumstances, how can we expect the federal government to impose higher premiums on Canadian workers and employers? Should we ask Canadians to incur a higher deficit in the UI fund? I think not.
In closing, I would like once again to acknowledge the hon. member's intentions in sponsoring this motion, but it is clear that his idea is simply impractical and detracts from the real purpose of the unemployment insurance program, which is to protect unemployed workers while they look for a job.

Private Members' Business

I would like to compliment my colleague from Restigouche- Chaleur for this initiative, an act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act for temporary community services.
The member from Calgary North began by saying that he saluted the initiative of the member for Restigouche-Chaleur as well-intentioned, and then in the end he sort of said that it was not practical. What is the purpose of this House of Commons if we are not here to craft and amend legislation? When we discover flaws in the legislation, what is wrong with having these legitimate debates where the government can perhaps show some good faith, and instead of just debating them in a token fashion, say: "Let's work together and we are going to get this amendment through". This bill is not going to shake the fiscal framework of this country. I was amused by the remark earlier of the member from Markham. His rationale was that by amending this bill, where would it lead to? It could lead to further amendments. I must be losing it, because I thought we were here to craft and amend legislation.
This week I had a constituent come in to my office and he talked about the flaw in the UI legislation related to adoptive parents, where adoptive parents do not get the same benefit as natural parents. I must have been asleep or something the day that particular piece of legislation went through. That is a real flaw in the legislation. I am going to be asking the Law Clerk if he will help me to prepare an amendment to the legislation.
I cannot believe that anyone on the government side is going to put forward an argument that because of the fiscal constraints we are under, we are going to have a different law for adoptive parents. That is just not good logic.
It seems to me that when we have an amendment like this, it is an opportunity for the government to practise what it has been preaching in the last two weeks. The government has been talking about putting some goodwill and spirit back into this country and showing that we are acting in a fair way.
Talk to Mr. Chretien about that.
I would be happy to talk to him about that.
He cannot support this bill.

He does support this bill. There they go again, Mr. Speaker. This idea of goodwill is only one way. They expect us on this side to wimp out on every piece of nonsense that goes on on that side of the House. It is like the government House leader when he talked about decorum. It is all words. He never meant it.
They talk about my leader. I think it is fair ball. We are all human. I think the Leader of the Opposition has basically said that the frustration that they are causing not only the people of Canada but us as members of Parliament from time to time is such that we sort of bolt.
Possibly trying to manipulate the destruction of the country.

The member for Calgary North now is really losing it. Here we are talking about a simple amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act and he is linking an amendment to this act and the destruction of the country. That is not really what it is all about. I cannot believe it.
The member for Restigouche-Chaleur has obviously been hearing from his constituents and has used the process of this House of Commons and there is not an ounce of goodwill. I am telling you right now, Mr. Speaker, here is a simple amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act where we are asking the government an easy thing. Do you know what is incredible about this? The minister responsible is from the same province, from New Brunswick and we cannot get these men and women to put some pressure on the minister. It is a ministerial stroke of the pen to amend this.
It is token goodwill. It is not even a big deal. But no, they get set in their ways and say that it is impractical, where would it lead to. Obviously I get a sense that there is not going to be a lot of movement over there. It is no wonder why sometimes we throw our hands up in
November 19, 1991

frustration and wonder what the heck we are doing in this House. I just hope that maybe there can be a moment of reflection on that side of the House that they will consider looking at this and consider the fact that fighting for amendments whether it is for volunteers like this, or even for the adoptive parents, rather than us coming to hit them on the head from time to time, why do they not show some initiative on their part and say: "Listen, there is a flaw in this legislation and we want an amendment. Let's get it through and on with it and let's figure out ways in which we can get people back to work".

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise this afternoon in relation to the approval process provided by the Government of Canada to the United States military for Trident nuclear submarines to pass through Canada's sovereign internal waters at Dixon Entrance.
The history of the boundary, the A-B line and this body of water which is sovereign and internal to Canada, is one of a trail of bullying, broken promises, treachery, deception, lies and treason, and it carries on to this very day.
On October 2 in the question that is being covered again this evening, I asked the Prime Minister why he and the government were proceeding to approve the transit of these U.S. nuclear submarines through Dixon Entrance. The Minister for International Trade responded for the Prime Minister and simply said, and I quote: "Discussions are ongoing".
In the August 28, 1991, cabinet document, which I will be providing today to Hansard, it says:
Given that a Govemor-in-Council decision is soon going to be
announced regarding the transit of nuclear submarines through
Dixon Entrance -
That quote makes it quite clear that a decision had already been reached, certainly within the bureaucracy, and I suspect at the ministerial and cabinet level as well. So I pursued it and on November 1, at page 4371 of Hansard, I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs:
Have there been submerged U.S. submarine transits of Dixon
Entrance in the past two years?
The minister said and I quote: "My understanding is no".
On October 30, the same minister announced an Order in Council providing consent for U.S. nuclear propelled submarines to pass submerged through Dixon

Entrance. It raises a very fundamental question, Mr. Speaker, of who is in charge? Who is in fact in charge? Is it really possible that on October 30 the Secretary of State for External Affairs would announce blanket prior consent for U.S. nuclear submarines to go through Dixon Entrance and actually expect members of the House of Commons and the Canadian public to believe that she had never been informed and simply did not know that the U.S. navy had been illegally transiting Dixon Entrance on a regular basis for the previous two years? I somehow think not.
We have to ask why was the deal hidden?
I would like to reflect for a moment on the words of the former secretary of state, the Right Hon. Joe Clark, as recorded March 23, 1987 at page 4447 of Hansard when he was questioned by the previous member for New Westminster-Coquitlam, Pauline Jewett, in relation to the polar sea and Arctic sovereignty. Ms. Jewett asked:
Can we have the assurance that some secretly negotiated agreement
will not be sprung on the Canadian public at that time?
Mr. Clark said the following:
The assurance is categoric. There will be no secret agreements
sprung upon anybody. I take very seriously, if I may say so, the
obligation on these matters with respect to the north.
He goes on to say that it is the practice of this government, which has asserted northern sovereignty, to consult extensively with all those Canadians who are interested.
There was no consultation. It was secret. There has been no environmental assessment and there must be because, as I pointed out before, in just one recent four-year period these very same U.S. nuclear submarines have been involved in over 400 accidents; 12 groundings, 50 collisions, 113 onboard fires, 14 onboard explosions and 31 onboard crew suicides.
The people of British Columbia and the people of my constituency deserve a risk assessment, an emergency preparedness assessment, a full environmental assessment and review that is public. This government cannot keep these kinds of issues secret. We deserve to know publicly what is going on.

speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we may
want to dispute with the hon. member some of the alleged facts he puts forward today.
One thing that there is not a dispute about and with which we agree with him totally is the sovereignty of the A-B line, the boundary between the United States and Canada in the upper coastline of British Columbia. That is indisputable. Canada has never wavered from that position. It is an internationally agreed upon boundary which is nearly 100 years old. That is Canada's boundary and there is no dispute about that.
There is a dispute, however, first of all, about the comparison he makes between this issue and the polar seas. That is not a NATO exercise, that is not a NORAD exercise, that was a sovereignty issue between Canada and the United States. The former Secretary of State for External Affairs was accurate and categorical in the statements he made on that issue.
This issue regarding submarine traffic in the Dixon Entrance has to do with our agreements with the United States through NATO and NORAD. It is not only U.S. subs that have gone there but other NATO subs have been there. So if I might put a pun on it, to polarize the issue as a Canada-U.S. issue is not accurate and it does not stand scrutiny under fact. To raise bogus alarmist stories about fires on these subs when he does not say whether it was an ash tray or a steak in the galley or sub-machinery related fires is alarmist and it is unconscionable for the member to do that.
I would say that yes, there is an agreement between Canada and the United States through the NATO agreement. Yes, there has been an environmental study conducted and, yes we are going to continue this. It is not a Canada-U.S. issue, it is a collective security issue which Canada plans to honour.

Mr. Speaker, the Kendall Company established a manufacturing plant in the city of Toronto about the year 1916. It moved in 1953 to East York which was then a suburb of the city of Toronto and is now one of the six cities that make up metropolitan Toronto.
Two years ago, Kendall employed some 700 persons in its East York plant manufacturing bandages, dressings and medical supplies. Two years ago our government gave Kendall $1 million to move its East York operation to Peterborough, Ontario and to establish a brand new
November 19, 1991

manufacturing operation there. With Canadian taxpayers' money, including the tax money of those 700 employees in East York, Kendall closed its East York plant. It laid off 700 people, established a new manufacturing plant in Peterborough and hired another 200 people there. That was two years ago.
In September of this year Kendall announced that it was closing its new manufacturing facility in Peterborough altogether, laying off 165 employees and moving its production to the United States. I wish this was an isolated case but it is not.
Our own government says that over the last two years there has been a net reduction in manufacturing employment in Canada of about 195,000 jobs. In fairness, thousands of jobs are lost every year whether it is in good times or bad.
In fairness, over four million Canadians change their jobs every year. In fairness, manufacturing employment as a percentage of the labour force has actually been declining since 1950 when it was 26 per cent and today it is only 16 per cent. In fairness, the United States also lost about a million manufacturing jobs over the last two years. And in fairness, in spite of the loss of manufacturing jobs there has been a net increase in the total number of jobs here in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, you and I know that none of that helps if you have lost your job, if you have received your lay-off notice or if you are afraid that you are going to lose your job or somebody in your family is going to be losing their job very soon.
What is the government going to do about it? I have suggested that we can stimulate demand, create jobs and get the economy moving again by perhaps using the 5 per cent down payment, the registered retirement savings plan as down payment, lowering the differential on the interest rates between Canadian and U.S. dollars and providing short-term loans, not grants, to manufacturing businesses that need help to survive in the short term.
So far the government has refused to act on any of these suggestions. I have not heard any brilliant ideas from the government except: "We will keep lowering interest rates". Interest rates going down did not solve the problem in the 1930s and so far it has not solved the problem today.
What does the minister have in mind?
Adjournment
Mr. Bill Domm (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister
for Science): Mr. Speaker, first let me point out that when Kendall announced some two or two and a half years ago that it was closing its operation employing some 700 people, at that time IRDP was in place, the Industrial Regional Development Program, and Peterborough was eligible for that funding to locate industries in an area of high unemployment.
I am happy to report that as a result of IRDP, which we no longer have and maybe I could support my hon. friend in reinstating IRDP, 26 projects located in the Peterborough area representing a capital investment of some $8,836 million.
In my conversations with Kendall today in Peterborough it advised me that it is retaining its own factory and property. It is not putting it up for sale. It is employing over the next number of years a minimum of 107 people and will be engaged in the process of distributing coast to coast in Canada out of the Peterborough operation with
80.000	square feet of space being used.
In addition, it found it necessary to rent the other
80.000	feet of space which it owned and is installing at the moment some high-tech equipment so it can handle a very involved cross-Canada distribution program. With modern telecommunications it is now able to receive phone calls from any hospital in Canada direct to that factory, and it is going to maintain warehouses in both Moncton and one other part of the country. It is retaining those outlets for distribution in Moncton and in the west.
I am pleased to announce that Kendall expects to continue its program. I can advise the member that the government has investigated the investment of $1 million and on a preliminary, cursory view it is prepared to recommend that it lived up to its agreements under the IRDP. It is not intended to-

Mr. Speaker, on June 101 gave notice of my intention to raise during the adjournment debate the issue I raised at the time.
On June 10 I asked the government what it intended to do about saving the jobs involved in manual sortation at the Cambellton post office. This question was further to a press release issued by the Canada Post Corporation on May 7, announcing measures to rationalize mail

November 19, 1991
Adjournment
processing which would eliminate more than half of the staff at the Campbellton Post Office.
The government's response was predictable. The minister showered me with platitudes about the use of technology to increase efficiency at Canada Post. However, he conveniently forgot to answer my question about job losses in a region that has a very high level of unemployment. When I waved a letter under his nose from the office of the president of the Canada Post Corporation, indicating that the latter had no intention of removing sorting operations from Campbellton, he again evaded the issue by referring to what the Liberal government did 10 years ago about political interference in the Canada Post Corporation.

The reason for my question on that date was that I had received a letter from Canada Post. Rather than read it all I will just read the last sentence. It says:
Dear Mr. Arseneault:
I can assure you that we have no plan to remove sorting operations
from Campbellton.
Following that there was a press release by Canada Post basically stating the opposite, telling us that there was going to be downgrading of sorting operations in a number of communities across Canada, Campbellton being one of them.
I immediately requested a meeting with Canada Post. In all fairness, I should say that Canada Post responded very quickly and came to the riding to meet with the member of Parliament, myself, and a number of other individuals. I want to be on record now as thanking Canada Post because as a result of that meeting there was a partial reversal of that decision.
However, I must still remind the government that I did have a commitment that there would be no loss whatsoever. A partial reversal in my mind is not good enough.
Specifically from the government we heard that the reasons for doing this was technology. I am not against technology but I ask: Does technology require that you have to go into a post office, buy a stamp and then go outside to mail it when the post office is open? Is that technology? Is technology the lack of mail boxes in rural Canada? Is technology closing post offices? Is technology rewarding your management for all the major cuts it has
been making across the land in Canada Post and trying to get back at the union members?
I hope that I will get a more direct answer this evening. I hope that Canada Post would plainly say that there would be no loss of positions at the Campbellton post office, because that was the original commitment.
In closing, I should say that I have another commitment from Canada Post in our riding. I was told that I would be informed of any changes in my riding with regard to Canada Post. I was just informed yesterday that effectively there has been a cutback at the Nash Creek post office, a reduction of hours for some employees. I would ask again that Canada Post reverse that cutback.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Shields (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I note with interest the hon. member's concern regarding Canada Post Corporation's recent announcement with respect to mail processing in the town of Campbellton.
He complains that the mail processing will be removed from the town and that people will lose their jobs and he asks that the government intervene in this matter.
I am truly surprised that the hon. member would suggest that the government intervene in the postal operation, when it was agreed by all three parties in 1981, and perhaps he is not familiar with this, that Canada Post should be free of political interference. The corporation has come a long way from when it was a debt ridden burden on the Canadian taxpayer, costing Canadians hundreds of millions of dollars. As a matter of fact, it has just recorded its third straight year of profitable operations.
Part of Canada Post's success story can be attributed to the operational efficiency achieved through such initiatives as process rationalization. This program is not new. In September 1990 Canada Post implemented mail processing changes to make more efficient use of its work force, its equipment and facilities as well as improved transportation links throughout the country. This streamlining ensures delivery standards are maintained or exceeded. The program is presently operating successfully in some 100 Canadian communities and now the corporation is planning to proceed with similar measures in an additional 54 communities later this year. More mail will be consolidated for processing and fed
November 19, 1991

directly into mechanized plants for maximum efficiency and faster sorting and distribution.
In some communities such as Campbellton twin mailboxes will be introduced so that the customers can separate their local and forward mail, which is mail bound for all other destinations. The mail separation eliminates one step in mail handling and the forward mail will go directly to Saint John for mechanized sorting while the local mail will continue to be processed in Campbellton.
I would just like to close and say with respect to any reduction in the number of jobs as a result of the implementation of this program, Canadians can rest assured that work force changes at Canada Post are being managed in a responsible manner.

Mr. Speaker, I first brought this issue to the attention of the Minister of Finance over a year ago before the GST became law.
I began receiving calls and letters from my constituents who are naturally upset by the discriminatory practice that they were receiving from the government on the GST.
I tried to to explain to the minister that it was unfair to have a double standard in which urban residents can get an unlimited amount of water GST free, whereas GST on water and on basic necessities in rural Canada was being applied.
However, on February 6, 1991, the then Minister of Finance indicated: "No GST will apply to the supply of potable water". Such was not the case. Changes were made and rural Canada continued to suffer under the burden of this regressive tax.
In response to the overwhelming calls from my constituents, I asked the minister in the House on June 11,1991 to immediately correct this serious injustice to rural Canada.
The present Minister of Finance replied in a letter to me of June 13, 1991 indicating: "The GST as amended on March 27 exempts the supply of unbottled water when provided by a municipality or by an organization designated as a municipality for the purposes of that supply".
The government's tune had changed and it continues to try to convince rural Canadians that all is fair, that the
Adjournment
problem has been solved. It has not. Rather, the government's proposed solution to the unfair tax of water used by rural Canadians served only to shift the tax discrimination from rural residents to rural water suppliers. Water suppliers can apply to become a designated municipality so that they do not have to charge GST to the customers. However, as a municipality the suppliers can only get 57.14 per cent of their input tax credits as opposed to the full 100 per cent able to be acquired by other small businesses. Hence, the designation of a water hauler as a municipality can result in the customers having access to tax free water, but the water haulers must bear the brunt of this and they must lose their full GST rebate which all others enjoy.
This uncertainty is a discrimination and it is totally unacceptable. This convoluted legislation is pitting water hauler against water hauler, antagonizing and frustrating customers and causing a paper nightmare to claim the input credits. Furthermore, to try to get a straight answer out of Revenue Canada on this is next to impossible. The minister was bound to know that a tax like the GST would run into some snags, and this is one of them. The real crime is that he can easily solve this problem. All he has to do is bring in amending legislation to zero rate bulk supplies of water. In the larger scheme of things this may seem like a little thing, but I tell you it has meant hardship in rural Canada and it has meant hardship among rural water haulers. The hardship and discontent is clearly demonstrated by the well over 6,000 signatures I have received from rural petitioners. Still I am having numbers of petitioners and numbers of petitions come in.
Water is a basic necessity of life, and I would ask the Minister of Finance to immediately rectify this unfair discrimination in rural Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I would first of all point out to the hon. member that the Minister of Finance is a member from rural Canada who understands water supply very well.
The member for Haldimand-Norfolk has criticized the GST for creating an inequity in the treatment of water supplies between rural and urban residents. The member believes that residents of rural areas who do not have access to municipal distribution systems are required to pay GST for their water while city dwellers receive water tax free.

Adjournment
Let me clarify the policy in this matter. The goods and services tax, as amended on March 27, exempts a supply of unbottled water when provided by a municipality or by an organization designated as a municipality for the purpose of supplying water. An independent water supplier, for example a private water utility or a bulk water supplier, may apply to Revenue Canada Customs and Excise Division for such designation. Its sales of water will then be exempt. Like municipalities, it will then also be entitled to a 57 per cent partial rebate of GST for tax paid on inputs, including vehicles, equipment and fuel. Accordingly the policy provides for consistent treatment of water supplies in urban and rural areas. Of course, a private supplier may choose not to apply for designation as a municipality. In those instances, it would be required to collect and remit GST and will be entitled to full input tax credit. This may be an appropriate result where the clients of the supplier, that is farmers purchasing irrigation water, are themselves able to claim input tax credits for GST paid.
However, in other circumstances private suppliers would most likely want to take advantage of the exemption, thereby ensuring that rural residents receive their water on the same tax exempt basis as urban residents.
A recommendation was made by the hon. member for Haldimand-Norfolk that the supply of water from bulk water suppliers should be zero rated, that is removing tax on the supply and at the same time giving suppliers full input tax credits. However, that would not provide equitable treatment of bulk suppliers and municipal suppliers.
The legislation allows consistent treatment of the supply of water to both urban and rural residents. However, we recognize that there have been difficulties informing water haulers of this policy, and as a result there has been some confusion with respect to the treatment of supplies of water to rural residents. Consequently, we are looking at ways to simplify the application of the exemption in this area. Maybe the hon. member, since he is concerned about this, will help spread the word.

Mr. Speaker, last June 17 I raised an immigration issue of significant importance with respect to how our immigration procedures are handled and how we assure that the religious rights and freedoms guaranteed by the Charter of Rights and Freedoms are respected.
The matter clearly also affects the individuals whose circumstances prompted my question. Specifically, four Sikh priests denied status in Canada were facing deportation.
Forty thousand members of the Khalsa Dabar Sikh Temple in Mississauga were subsequently compelled to go to the courts to secure for their priests the very same rights guaranteed to all priests and religious ministers both under the Immigration Act and its regulations.
For example, directives from the Quebec region immigration office guarantee that priests can request a credible basis refugee claim without a formal interview or hearing. But these four were denied that opportunity. The minister was brusque in responding to a reasonable request for intervention. First he declared that the priests should simply get out. He was precipitous, he was wrong and worse, he was inflammatory.
Second, he refused in this House to be involved or to comment claiming that this case was before the courts. Yet no court action had begun. His involvement had been asked so that a court action could be avoided.
Third, after I advised him that the priests together had 12 more administrative procedures before refugee hearings, he lashed out with personal attacks on this member engaging in diversionary tactics because he was not in possession of the facts.
He owes Canadians the responsibility to stay informed. His perverse inaction is creating unnecessary turbulence in the lives of individual priests and their parishioners. To date the immigration department has refused to deal with the questions of religion and priesthood. It has forced the priests to go into a refugee system to secure status, thus denying Sikhs the same access to their priests as Catholics, Protestants and others have to their own.
November 19, 1991

The actions of the department means in effect that it does not recognize the Sikh religion. Without their priests Sikhs cannot enjoy the guarantees of religious freedom under section 2 of the charter. The multicultural character of Canada referred to under section 27 can no longer apply to them. The equality provisions under section 15 ring hollow for them.
How can the minister justify depriving Sikhs of these basic freedoms?
[Editor's Note: Member spoke in Punjabi, translated as
follows:]

This is an affront to Sikh faith and to Canadians of Punjabi origin who practise the Sikh religion. They live by the precepts of their founder, the Guru Nanek, who called for peace among men, equality between genders and among races, respect for individual rights and differences, who preached humility, industry and the concept of community.
Mr. Speaker, these are admirable Canadian values and as a country we should support those who advance them there and everywhere.

Yes, and yet the minister is prepared to send these priests to a country where they will be clearly in danger. International press reports, UN resolutions, Amnesty International, among other impartial observers point to the fact that the deportation to the Punjab will lead to certain danger for the applicants.
It is time the minister acted to ensure that the Sikh community in Canada has a real chance to live in dignity. It cannot continue to thrive or to do so without figures central to Sikh religion and to culture, that is their priests.
I urge the minister to stop waffling, stop dallying, to get involved, intervene and ensure that they have an opportunity to stay in Canada and to minister to the parishioners of Sikh faith in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Shields (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of Employment and Immigration,
Adjournment
I wish to respond in greater detail to the questions raised by my hon. friend from Eglinton-Lawrence.
As the hon. member well knows, the backlog clearance program for Bill C-55, Canada's refugee determination system, is among the most generous refugee protection systems in the world and he should acknowledge that.
Both systems are administered uniformly across the country. Decisions are made by independent, and I stress, are made by independent decision makers and each case is reviewed on humanitarian and compassionate grounds. Nevertheless, Canada's refugee determination systems were never intended to serve as another route for immigration. That should be made very clear.
Our goal is to provide Canada's protection to those who genuinely need it and to deal firmly but fairly with those who do not. It should be noted that the four individuals referred to by the hon. member all made refugee claims. They have the right to have their claims determined. In fact, under Canadian law there is an absolute obligation to deal with their claims. It should also be noted that Employment and Immigration Canada has been working with Canadian congregations including the Sikhs and foreign clergy and religious workers for a long time.
There are well established procedures in place to facilitate the admission of foreign religious workers either as immigrants or temporary workers. Officials of Employment and Immigration would be pleased to assist the congregation of Khalsa Dabar Temple should they wish to bring in foreign religious workers according to the requirements of Canadian law.
Similarly, if a refugee claim is rejected and a removal order issued, those same officials have no choice but to proceed with the removal. That is as the law requires. Canadians expect as much.
